explanation: B-cells differentiate into plasma cells which secrete antibodies into bodily fluids. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary role of cytotoxic T-cells in the immune response?

options.A: Secreting large amounts of free-floating antibodies
options.B: Forming the physical outer skin and mucosal barriers
options.C: Directly destroying virus-infected or cancerous host cells
options.D: Producing histamine to trigger acute allergic reactions

explanation: Cytotoxic T-cells identify and induce apoptosis in abnormal or infected host cells. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h5)

question: What is the main function of the membrane attack complex formed by complement proteins?

options.A: Producing antibodies in response to viral antigens
options.B: Releasing histamine to trigger smooth muscle contraction
options.C: Puncturing holes in bacterial cell membranes to cause lysis
options.D: Transporting oxygen molecules to damaged local tissues

explanation: The membrane attack complex drills channels into target cells, causing fluid to rush in and lyse the cell. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h6)

question: What process involves complement proteins coating a pathogen to make it easier for phagocytes to engulf?

options.A: Vasodilation
options.B: Opsonization
options.C: Apoptosis
options.D: Chemotaxis

explanation: Opsonization marks pathogens with proteins so phagocytic cells can easily recognize and swallow them. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h6)

question: What happens when immune tolerance mechanisms fail within the body?

options.A: Neutrophils multiply uncontrollably without any microbial trigger
options.B: The body becomes completely defenceless against simple viruses
options.C: Primary lymphoid organs immediately shut down all cell production
options.D: Autoimmune disorders develop due to attacks on self-tissues

explanation: A failure in tolerance causes the immune system to treat healthy host cells as foreign invaders. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h7)

question: Which term describes the process of eliminating self-reactive lymphocytes during maturation?

options.A: Inflammatory cascade
options.B: Cellular chemotaxis
options.C: Active opsonization
options.D: Central tolerance

explanation: Central tolerance removes self-reactive lymphocytes while they develop in primary lymphoid organs. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h7)

question: Why are routine immunization programs like the EPI important for community health?

options.A: They induce adaptive immunity and immunological memory against common diseases
options.B: They permanently eliminate the need for physical anatomical barriers
options.C: They replace damaged white blood cells lost during severe infections
options.D: They instantly destroy all bacteria present on the skin surface

explanation: Vaccines safely expose the immune system to antigens, priming memory cells for future defense. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h8)

question: Which clinical laboratory result helps nurses evaluate the severity of an ongoing infection?

options.A: Total daily fluid intake volume
options.B: Leukocyte differential count
options.C: Serum electrolyte balance
options.D: Fasting blood glucose level

explanation: Analyzing the types and numbers of white blood cells provides insight into the body's immune response. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T1#GNS123_U4_T1_h8)

question: What are the two primary categories of human immune defence mechanisms?

options.A: Primary and secondary immunity
options.B: Innate and adaptive immunity
options.C: Active and passive immunity
options.D: Cellular and humoral immunity

explanation: Human immunity is broadly split into innate mechanisms present from birth and adaptive mechanisms developed over time. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h1)

question: What is the primary characteristic of innate immunity compared to adaptive immunity?

options.A: It targets specific pathogenic antigens
options.B: It creates long-term immunological memory
options.C: It provides immediate, non-specific protection
options.D: It takes weeks to become fully active

explanation: Innate immunity acts right away against any foreign invader without targeting specific molecular signatures. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h1)

question: Which structure forms the primary physical barrier against pathogen invasion in the human body?

options.A: The capillary endothelium
options.B: The skin
options.C: The mucous membrane
options.D: The lymphatic vessels

explanation: The keratinized cells of the skin create a tough, dry, and nearly impenetrable outer barrier. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h2)

question: How do resident normal microbiota protect the human body from infection?

options.A: By competing with pathogens for space and nutrients
options.B: By producing specific antibodies against viral particles
options.C: By directly phagocytosing invading bacteria in tissues
options.D: By raising the local body temperature to cause fever

explanation: Normal flora occupy cellular binding sites and consume available resources, leaving little room for harmful microbes. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h2)

question: Which white blood cells are primarily responsible for the phagocytosis of invading pathogens?

options.A: Erythrocytes and thrombocytes
options.B: B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes
options.C: Neutrophils and macrophages
options.D: Basophils and eosinophils

explanation: Neutrophils and macrophages are professional phagocytes that engulf and destroy foreign cellular debris. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h3)

question: What is the primary function of natural killer cells in the second line of defence?

options.A: Secreting mucus to trap airborne dust particles
options.B: Forming hard clots to seal bleeding blood vessels
options.C: Producing high-affinity antibodies against bacteria
options.D: Destroying virus-infected cells and tumor cells

explanation: Natural killer cells identify abnormal cellular markers on stressed cells and trigger their programmed cell death. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h3)

question: Which chemical mediator is released by mast cells to cause vasodilation during inflammation?

options.A: Albumin
options.B: Hemoglobin
options.C: Insulin
options.D: Histamine

explanation: Mast cells degranulate and release histamine, which dilates local blood vessels and increases capillary permeability. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h4)

question: Why does localized tissue swelling occur during an acute inflammatory response?

options.A: Local nerve endings stop transmitting electrical signals
options.B: Red blood cells accumulate rapidly inside closed lymphatic vessels
options.C: Collagen fibers break down and release stored water molecules
options.D: Fluid and white blood cells leak into the interstitial space

explanation: Increased vascular permeability allows blood plasma and immune cells to move into the tissue, creating edema. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h4)

question: Where do T lymphocytes complete their maturation process before entering circulation?

options.A: The thymus
options.B: The spleen
options.C: The kidneys
options.D: The liver

explanation: T cells originate in the bone marrow but migrate to the thymus gland to mature and develop immunocompetence. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary role of B lymphocytes in adaptive immunity?

options.A: Directly lysing virus-infected host body cells
options.B: Differentiating into plasma cells to secrete antibodies
options.C: Releasing histamine to increase local blood flow
options.D: Forming physical barriers on the epithelial surface

explanation: Activated B cells transform into plasma factories that release specific antibodies to neutralize circulating antigens. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h5)

question: Which hormone elevated during chronic stress is known to suppress immune function?

options.A: Melatonin
options.B: Estrogen

options.D: Thyroxine

question: How does severe protein-energy malnutrition negatively impact the human immune system?

options.C: By causing permanent blockage of all peripheral lymphatic channels

question: Which laboratory value is most critical for a nurse to monitor when assessing an immunocompromised patient?

options.B: White blood cell count
options.C: Blood urea nitrogen
options.D: Red blood cell count

question: A patient with severe neutropenia is admitted to the ward. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?

options.A: Administering live attenuated viral vaccines to stimulate immunity
options.B: Placing fresh flowers in the room to brighten the clinical environment
options.C: Implementing strict protective isolation to minimize pathogen exposure
options.D: Encouraging frequent family visits to boost the patient's emotional state

question: What link in the chain of infection is broken by washing hands with soap and water?

options.A: Susceptible host
options.B: Infectious agent
options.C: Mode of transmission
options.D: Reservoir

explanation: Hand hygiene physically removes pathogens, interrupting their transfer from one surface or person to another. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h1)

question: A patient with a surgical wound acts as what part of the chain of infection?

options.A: Reservoir
options.B: Portal of entry
options.C: Mode of transmission
options.D: Infectious agent

explanation: The human body hosting the multiplying pathogen serves as the primary reservoir for infection. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why do standard antibiotics fail to cure viral infections?

options.A: Viruses live strictly inside human blood vessels
options.B: Viruses hide inside hard spores that block drugs
options.C: Viruses multiply too quickly for medications to reach them
options.D: Viruses lack the cell structures that antibiotics are designed to attack

explanation: Antibiotics target bacterial features like cell walls, which viruses do not have. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h2)

question: Which type of microorganism is single-celled and identified in the lab using Gram staining?

options.A: Virus

question: During which stage of infection are symptoms most vague and non-specific?

options.A: Prodromal stage
options.B: Illness stage
options.C: Convalescent stage
options.D: Incubation period

explanation: The prodromal stage features general feelings of being unwell before specific disease signs appear. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h3)

question: A patient exposed to measles shows no symptoms for ten days. What term describes this phase?

options.A: Incubation period
options.B: Illness stage
options.C: Prodromal stage
options.D: Convalescent stage

explanation: The incubation period spans from initial exposure up to the first emergence of clinical symptoms. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which defense mechanism is classified as part of the innate immune system?

options.A: Intact skin
options.B: T lymphocyte activity
options.C: Antibody production
options.D: Memory cell formation

explanation: Skin is a primary physical barrier present from birth, making it part of innate immunity. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the primary role of B lymphocytes during an infection?

options.A: Secreting chemical enzymes in tear fluid
options.B: Forming physical barriers on mucous membranes
options.C: Destroying infected host cells directly
options.D: Producing specific antibodies

explanation: B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antigen-specific antibodies into body fluids. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h4)

question: What laboratory result strongly suggests an active bacterial infection in a patient?

options.A: Decreased red blood cell count
options.B: Decreased platelet count
options.C: Elevated white blood cell count
options.D: Elevated serum sodium level

explanation: White blood cells multiply rapidly to combat invading pathogens, resulting in leukocytosis. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why is a wound culture and sensitivity test ordered before starting antibiotics?

options.A: To assess the nutritional status of the skin tissue
options.B: To identify the specific pathogen and the most effective drug
options.C: To check if the patient has chronic high blood pressure

explanation: Sensitivity testing ensures the prescribed medication targets the exact microorganism causing the infection. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h5)

question: Which personal protective equipment is required when caring for a patient on airborne precautions?

options.A: Clean gloves only
options.B: Sterile gown only
options.C: Surgical mask only

explanation: Airborne pathogens require specialized respiratory protection like an N95 mask to filter out microscopic particles. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h6)

question: When should standard precautions be applied in clinical practice?

explanation: Standard precautions are universal infection control practices used for all patients regardless of infection status. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is another common name for a nosocomial infection?

options.A: Primary systemic disease

options.D: Hospital-acquired infection

explanation: Nosocomial infections are acquired specifically within healthcare settings during the delivery of care. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why are hospital-acquired infections considered a major challenge in clinical practice?

options.A: They always resolve without any medical care
options.B: They only occur in surgical theatre suites
options.C: They increase patient hospital stay duration

explanation: These infections complicate recovery, leading to extended hospital admissions and higher treatment costs. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h1)

question: Which component represents where a pathogen normally lives and multiplies?

options.A: Portal of exit
options.B: Reservoir
options.C: Susceptible host
options.D: Infectious agent

explanation: A reservoir provides a suitable environment for microorganisms to survive, grow, and multiply. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h2)

question: What happens when a healthcare worker performs proper handwashing to break the infection cycle?

options.A: Mode of transmission is disrupted
options.B: Susceptible host is completely eliminated
options.C: Portal of entry becomes larger
options.D: Infectious agent changes its DNA structure

explanation: Hand hygiene stops pathogens from moving from one surface or person to another. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which body fluid is excluded from standard precaution assumptions regarding infectious agents?

options.A: Sweat
options.B: Urine

explanation: Standard precautions apply to all body fluids except sweat, unless it contains visible blood. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h3)

question: When should a nurse apply standard precautions in the ward?

options.A: Only when laboratory tests confirm a virus

explanation: Standard precautions are universal and apply to all patient care activities regardless of infection status. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h3)

question: Which respiratory protection is mandatory when caring for a patient with pulmonary tuberculosis?

options.A: Clear plastic face shield
options.B: Simple surgical mask
options.C: N95 respirator

explanation: Airborne pathogens like tuberculosis require high-filtration respirators to prevent inhaling small droplet nuclei. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h4)

question: A patient diagnosed with an infection spread through large respiratory droplets requires which precaution category?

options.A: Contact precautions
options.B: Airborne precautions
options.C: Droplet precautions
options.D: Universal reverse isolation

explanation: Droplet precautions stop pathogens that travel short distances through moisture expelled during coughing or sneezing. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h4)

question: What is the minimum recommended duration for washing visibly soiled hands with soap and water?

options.A: 2 to 3 minutes
options.B: 40 to 60 seconds

question: Why is soap and water preferred over alcohol hand rub when caring for a patient with Clostridium difficile?

options.B: Soap causes faster drying of skin oils
options.C: Soap has a pleasant fragrance for patients

explanation: Spore-forming organisms resist alcohol gels, requiring the physical washing action of soap and water. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is the very first item a nurse should put on when donning personal protective equipment?

options.A: Gloves

options.C: Gown
options.D: Face mask

explanation: The gown is put on first to cover clothing, followed by respiratory protection, eye protection, and gloves. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h6)

question: Why should gloves be removed first when taking off personal protective equipment after patient care?

options.A: The gown cannot be untied with gloves on

question: Where should the urine collection bag be positioned relative to the patient's bladder?

question: A nurse needs to prevent a catheter-associated urinary tract infection. What action is most appropriate?

question: Where should used hypodermic needles be disposed of immediately after injection?

question: Why is recapping used injection needles strongly discouraged in clinical settings?

options.B: It wastes valuable nursing shift time

question: Who should nurses report a sudden cluster of hospital infections to?

options.A: Infection control committee
options.B: Patient relative association
options.C: Hospital catering department
options.D: Local pharmacy storefront

explanation: The infection control committee investigates outbreaks and implements facility-wide prevention strategies. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h9)

question: Why is early nursing surveillance vital for infection control in the ward?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any laboratory blood tests
options.B: It reduces the cost of hospital building maintenance
options.C: It prevents patients from eating restricted foods

question: What defines a re-emerging infectious disease in a population?

question: Why is the distinction between emerging and re-emerging infections important for nurses?

options.C: It determines whether the patient requires mandatory surgical intervention

question: The rapid spread of infectious diseases across continents is primarily driven by what factor?

options.A: Stricter international quarantine laws

question: Deforestation contributes to the emergence of new infections by doing what?

question: Lassa fever is primarily transmitted to humans through contact with what animal vector?

question: Airborne transmission differs from droplet transmission because airborne pathogens are spread via what mechanism?

question: What is the primary role of a vector in infectious disease transmission?

question: Which symptom is commonly observed during the early stage of many emerging viral infections?

question: Why is proper specimen collection and handling vital when dealing with dangerous pathogens?

question: Cohorting patients on an infectious disease ward involves which of the following strategies?

question: When is antiviral therapy like ribavirin most effective for treating Lassa fever?

question: Why is meticulous fluid balance monitoring essential during supportive care for severe infections?

question: What is the primary purpose of public health disease surveillance?

question: A nurse suspects a case of a rare notifiable haemorrhagic fever in the ward. What action should be taken next?

question: Which cellular receptor does the SARS-CoV-2 virus bind to when entering human cells?

question: A severe 'cytokine storm' in COVID-19 patients commonly leads to which lung complication?

question: Which personal protective equipment (PPE) is essential when performing procedures that generate aerosols on a COVID-19 patient?

question: How does the SARS-CoV-2 virus primarily spread from person to person?

options.C: Respiratory droplets and aerosols
options.D: Transplacental maternal transfer

question: An oxygen saturation level dropping below what percentage on room air indicates severe COVID-19 illness?

question: What is the standard diagnostic test used to confirm an active COVID-19 infection?

options.D: Complete blood count with differential

question: Which blood test result is commonly seen in patients with an acute COVID-19 infection?

options.C: Basophilia
options.D: Thrombocytosis

question: What does the term 'silent hypoxia' mean in COVID-19 patients?

question: A COVID-19 patient has a normal breathing rate and says they feel fine, but their pulse oximeter reads 86 percent on room air. What is the immediate nursing action?

options.D: Broad-spectrum antibiotics

question: Why are blood thinners (anticoagulants) routinely given to hospitalized patients with moderate to severe COVID-19?

options.C: To maintain normal blood pressure during a cytokine storm
options.D: To prevent dangerous blood clots driven by hypercoagulability

question: What is the main medical benefit of turning a patient with severe COVID-19 onto their stomach (prone position)?

options.B: Improves ventilation-perfusion matching in the lungs

question: When is a mechanical ventilator usually used for a patient with worsening COVID-19?

question: Persistent COVID-19 symptoms lasting beyond what timeframe are classified as Long COVID?
