explanation: Todd's paresis is a temporary weakness in a specific part of the body following a seizure that wears off after a few hours. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h5)

question: Which diagnostic tool is primarily used to record abnormal brain electrical activity?

options.A: Electrocardiogram
options.B: Electromyogram
options.C: Echocardiogram
options.D: Electroencephalogram

explanation: An EEG measures voltage fluctuations resulting from ionic current within the neurons of the brain. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h6)

question: Why do doctors order a brain scan (neuroimaging) when someone has a new-onset seizure?

options.A: To assess heart rhythm abnormalities
options.B: To detect physical brain damage, scars, or tumors
options.C: To measure exact salt levels in the blood
options.D: To evaluate how well oxygen is moving through the lungs

explanation: Imaging scans like an MRI help find physical issues like strokes, scars, or tumors that may be causing the seizures. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h6)

question: What is the main medical treatment used to manage epilepsy day-to-day?

options.A: Intravenous electrolyte infusions
options.B: Daily immunosuppressive drugs
options.C: Anti-seizure medications
options.D: Long-term antibiotic therapy

explanation: Anti-seizure medications are the main treatment used to calm electrical activity and prevent future seizures. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h7)

question: When is surgery usually considered for a patient with epilepsy?

options.A: When medication side effects are extremely mild
options.B: Immediately following the first unprovoked episode
options.C: Only when an EEG test is completely normal
options.D: When seizures cannot be controlled by multiple medications

explanation: Surgery is kept as an option for drug-resistant epilepsy when medications fail and a clear seizure source can be safely removed. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h7)

question: What duration of continuous seizure activity defines status epilepticus?

options.A: Less than one minute
options.B: Exactly thirty seconds
options.C: Longer than five minutes
options.D: More than two hours

explanation: Seizures lasting beyond five minutes carry a high risk of permanent neuronal damage and define status epilepticus. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h8)

question: What is the most important immediate nursing action during an active convulsive seizure?

options.A: Give the patient water immediately to prevent dehydration
options.B: Force a padded wooden spatula into the oral cavity
options.C: Attempt to physically hold down all moving limbs
options.D: Protect the patient from injury and keep the airway clear

explanation: Safety comes first: clear dangerous objects, turn the patient onto their side to keep the airway open, and never force anything into their mouth. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h8)

question: Which lifestyle factor is a very common trigger for breakthrough seizures in epilepsy patients?

options.A: Drinking clean water
options.B: Eating balanced meals
options.C: Regular moderate exercise
options.D: Not getting enough sleep

explanation: Poor rest or sleep deprivation lowers the brain's seizure threshold, making breakthrough seizures much more likely. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h9)

question: Why is psychosocial support so important in the overall care of an epilepsy patient?

options.A: To eliminate the need for regular EEG testing
options.B: To replace the requirement for daily medication
options.C: To permanently cure underlying brain malformations
options.D: To help them cope with social stigma and feelings of isolation

explanation: Psychosocial support helps patients deal with the emotional weight, anxiety, and social stigma that often come with a chronic condition. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T9#GNS222_U4_T9_h9)

question: Why are the testes located outside the main body cavity in the scrotum?

options.A: To produce testosterone for secondary sex traits
options.B: To store mature sperm cells before ejaculation
options.C: To keep the testes cooler than core body temperature
options.D: To secrete fluid that forms the bulk of semen

explanation: You've got this! Sperm production works best at a slightly lower temperature than our normal body heat. That is why nature designed the scrotum to hang outside the body to keep the testes nice and cool. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which part of the penis directly wraps around and surrounds the urethra?

options.A: Dartos muscle layer
options.B: Corpus spongiosum
options.C: Corpora cavernosa
options.D: Tunica albuginea

explanation: Great job thinking through the anatomy! The corpus spongiosum is the single column of spongy tissue that houses and protects the urethra as it runs down to the tip. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h1)

question: Where exactly inside the testes are sperm cells made?

options.A: Leydig cells
options.B: Seminiferous tubules
options.C: Tunica albuginea
options.D: Epididymis head

explanation: Think of the seminiferous tubules as tiny, packed-together factories inside the testes where germ cells constantly grow and transform into brand new sperm! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is the main job of the Leydig cells found in the testes?

options.A: Protecting developing germ cells from immune attack
options.B: Providing nutritional support to immature spermatids
options.C: Transporting mature sperm out of the lobules
options.D: Producing and secreting the hormone testosterone

explanation: You're doing great! Leydig cells hang out right between the sperm-producing tubes and are responsible for pumping out testosterone, the key male hormone. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h2)

question: What happens to sperm when they hang out in the epididymis?

options.A: To allow sperm to mature and gain swimming ability
options.B: To cool down the testes during physical exertion
options.C: To filter out abnormal sperm cells using white blood cells
options.D: To add fructose-rich fluid to the seminal mixture

explanation: Think of the epididymis as a training ground! Newly made sperm aren't ready to swim yet; they spend time here resting, maturing, and learning how to swim. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h3)

question: How do sperm travel upward through the long vas deferens during ejaculation?

options.A: By beating their flagella very rapidly
options.B: By suction created by the prostate gland
options.C: By smooth muscle peristaltic contractions
options.D: By gravity pulling them down into the urethra

explanation: Just like food moves down your gut, the walls of the vas deferens use wave-like muscle squeezes (peristalsis) to push sperm smoothly along their journey. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which male reproductive gland adds the most fluid volume to semen?

options.A: Seminal vesicles
options.B: Prostate gland
options.C: Testicular interstitium
options.D: Bulbourethral glands

explanation: Spot on! The seminal vesicles are generous contributors, providing about 60% of semen fluid along with sugary fructose to give the sperm energy. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h4)

question: Why do the bulbourethral glands release a clear mucus right before ejaculation?

options.A: To neutralize any leftover acid from urine in the urethra
options.B: To provide the main energy source for sperm motility
options.C: To activate sperm flagella for faster swimming
options.D: To cause the semen to clot firmly inside the vagina

explanation: Urine is quite acidic and can harm delicate sperm. This clever little mucus fluid cleanses the urethra path first so the sperm can pass safely! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which hormone signals the Leydig cells in the testes to make testosterone?

options.A: Luteinizing hormone (LH)
options.B: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
options.C: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)
options.D: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)

explanation: You've got this! Luteinizing hormone (LH) travels from the brain's pituitary gland down to the testes, giving the green light for testosterone production. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h5)

question: How would you explain a negative feedback loop of hormones to a curious patient?

options.A: It allows the brain to control your heart rate and breathing rate simultaneously.
options.B: It prevents the testes from ever changing in size throughout your lifetime.
options.C: It stops the body from producing too much testosterone when levels are already high.
options.D: It ensures that the pituitary gland stops working completely during physical rest.

explanation: Think of it like an air conditioner thermostat! When hormone levels get high enough, a signal goes back to the brain to slow things down so the body doesn't overproduce. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T1#GNS311_U1_T1_h5)

question: Which gland releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone to trigger the female reproductive cycle?

options.A: The anterior pituitary gland
options.B: The adrenal cortex
options.C: The hypothalamus
options.D: The posterior pituitary gland

explanation: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone is synthesized and released by the hypothalamus in the brain to kick off the hormonal cascade. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h1)

question: What usually happens when the delicate hormonal balance of the female reproductive system is disrupted?

options.A: Secondary sex characteristics reverse themselves instantly
options.B: Estrogen production permanently stops across all age groups
options.C: The reproductive organs immediately undergo complete atrophy
options.D: It can lead to issues ranging from irregular periods to more serious health concerns

explanation: Think of hormones like a delicate chain reaction! When one part is out of balance, it can throw off the whole cycle, leading to skipped periods or other reproductive challenges. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h1)

question: What is the medical term for abnormally heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding?

options.A: Oligomenorrhea
options.B: Dysmenorrhea
options.C: Menorrhagia
options.D: Amenorrhea

explanation: Menorrhagia describes periods that are excessively heavy or last longer than normal, often draining the body's iron stores. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h2)

question: A patient with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is most likely to show which group of signs?

options.A: High male hormone levels, failure to release eggs regularly, and insulin resistance
options.B: Heavy bleeding, low blood pressure, and severe weight loss
options.C: Complete absence of pubic hair and early menopause
options.D: Frequent fever, pelvic pain, and purulent vaginal discharge

explanation: PCOS is a very common hormonal condition. It usually involves high levels of androgens (male hormones), irregular ovulation, and trouble handling insulin properly. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h2)

question: What is a cystocele?

options.A: Benign smooth muscle tumors growing inside the myometrium
options.B: Bulging of the bladder into the anterior vaginal wall
options.C: Herniation of the rectum into the posterior vaginal canal
options.D: Downward displacement of the uterus through the cervix

explanation: A cystocele happens when the supportive tissue between a woman's bladder and vaginal wall weakens, allowing the bladder to sag into the vagina. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h3)

question: Why do pelvic organ prolapse conditions often lead to problems with urination?

options.A: Estrogen surges cause the bladder to double in physical size
options.B: Infection destroys the smooth muscle tissue of the ureters
options.C: The kidneys stop producing urine due to chronic pelvic pressure
options.D: The shifted position of the organs changes normal urine flow mechanics

explanation: When supportive pelvic structures weaken and sag, organs like the bladder shift out of place. This makes it hard to empty the bladder fully, leading to frequent urges or retention. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h3)

question: Which germs are the most common causes of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)?

options.A: Candida albicans and Trichomonas vaginalis
options.B: Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus
options.C: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
options.D: Human papillomavirus and Herpes simplex virus

explanation: PID usually happens when sexually transmitted bacteria travel upward from the vagina and cervix into the uterus and fallopian tubes. Always good to remember for clinicals! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h4)

question: A young female patient has lower abdominal pain and cries out in severe pain when the nurse moves her cervix during a pelvic exam. What is the most likely condition?

options.A: Uterine fibroids
options.B: Primary dysmenorrhea
options.C: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
options.D: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

explanation: That intense pain when moving the cervix is called 'cervical motion tenderness' (or a positive chandelier sign), and it's a classic red flag for PID. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h4)

question: Persistent infection with high-risk strains of which common virus is the primary cause of cervical cancer?

options.A: Epstein-Barr Virus
options.B: Human Papillomavirus
options.C: Human Immunodeficiency Virus
options.D: Cytomegalovirus

explanation: High-risk types of HPV can cause gradual changes in the cells of the cervix. Over time, these changes can turn cancerous if not caught early by a Pap smear. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why is ovarian cancer so often diagnosed at an advanced stage?

options.A: Patients refuse pelvic examinations until pain becomes unbearable
options.B: Early symptoms are vague and easily mistaken for normal tummy trouble or gas
options.C: Tumors spread exclusively through the lymphatic system
options.D: There are no reliable blood tests or imaging studies available

explanation: Ovarian cancer is tricky because early signs like bloating, mild fullness, or tummy ache look just like common digestive issues, so people often ignore them at first. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h5)

question: What tool does a doctor use to look closely at abnormal cervical tissue under a special magnifying lens?

options.A: Transvaginal ultrasound
options.B: Hysterosalpingography
options.C: Laparoscopy
options.D: Colposcopy

explanation: A colposcopy uses a special magnifying scope to take a closer look at the cervix, vagina, and vulva, usually following up on an abnormal Pap smear result. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h6)

question: What is the main reason a patient would have a hysterosalpingography (HSG) procedure done?

options.A: To measure circulating levels of follicle-stimulating hormone
options.B: To check if the fallopian tubes are open and examine the inside of the uterus
options.C: To visualize ovarian cysts and measure their exact physical dimensions
options.D: To scrape the endometrial lining for suspected malignant cells

explanation: During an HSG, a special dye is gently put into the uterus while taking X-rays. It helps doctors see if the fallopian tubes are blocked or clear. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T10#GNS311_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which specific cells in the testes are responsible for making testosterone?

options.A: Seminiferous tubules
options.B: Bulbourethral glands
options.C: Cells of Leydig
options.D: Epididymis

explanation: Great job! The interstitial cells of Leydig are found inside the testes and do the heavy lifting of making testosterone. Keep it up! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h1)

question: What is the main job of the fluid made by the seminal vesicles?

options.A: Storing mature sperm cells
options.B: Nourishing sperm with fructose
options.C: Lubricating the urethra
options.D: Neutralizing acidic urine

explanation: You've got this! Seminal vesicle fluid is packed with fructose, giving sperm the energy boost they need to swim toward the egg. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h1)

question: What actually happens to the prostate gland in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)?

options.A: Non-cancerous cell overgrowth
options.B: Infection-driven tissue necrosis
options.C: Malignant tumor invasion
options.D: Fibrotic tissue shrinking

explanation: Spot on! 'Benign' means non-cancerous. In BPH, the prostate cells simply overgrow, which is very common as men age. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h2)

question: If an older male patient has an enlarged prostate (BPH), what urinary symptom is he most likely to complain about?

options.A: A weak and slow urinary stream
options.B: Total absence of urine production
options.C: Inability to control bowel movements
options.D: Severe pain during bladder filling

explanation: Makes total sense, right? When the prostate grows, it presses on the urethra like a pinched garden hose, making the urine flow slow and weak. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is a major sign that sets acute bacterial prostatitis apart from chronic prostate issues?

options.A: Gradual hair loss on the legs
options.B: Sudden high fever and chills
options.C: Enlarged painless lymph nodes
options.D: Completely painless urination

explanation: Spot on. Acute infections hit hard and fast! Patients usually run a high fever and feel very sick, unlike chronic cases. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why is it so important to figure out the exact type of prostatitis a patient has?

options.A: It indicates that immediate surgical removal of the prostate is needed
options.B: It prevents the future development of benign prostatic hyperplasia
options.C: It proves whether the patient has concurrent testicular cancer
options.D: It dictates whether antibiotics or non-infectious management is required

explanation: Brilliant! Bacterial infections need antibiotics, while other types of pelvic pain need a totally different, non-infectious treatment plan. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why is testicular torsion treated as an absolute medical emergency?

options.A: It causes irreversible damage to the prostate gland
options.B: Loss of blood supply can lead to tissue death within hours
options.C: It always leads to permanent systemic high blood pressure
options.D: It immediately spreads severe infection to the kidneys

explanation: You nailed it. When the cord twists, it cuts off blood flow. If we don't fix it right away, the testicle can die. Every minute counts! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h4)

question: During a physical exam for a patient with testicular torsion, which reflex is usually missing?

options.A: Cremasteric reflex
options.B: Patellar reflex
options.C: Gag reflex
options.D: Babinski reflex

explanation: Correct! Normally, stroking the inner thigh makes the testicle rise (cremasteric reflex). In torsion, that reflex is completely absent. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h4)

question: Testicular cancer is most commonly diagnosed in which age group?

options.A: Young men aged 15 to 35
options.B: Middle-aged men aged 50 to 65
options.C: Pre-pubertal boys under 10
options.D: Elderly men over 75 years

explanation: Good to know! Unlike many other cancers, testicular cancer hits younger guys, which is why teaching self-exams to this group is so vital. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h5)

question: What is the most common early sign of testicular cancer?

options.A: Sudden severe pain accompanied by a high fever
options.B: Recurrent urinary tract infections and visible blood
options.C: A painless, firm lump inside the testicle
options.D: Painful swelling of the entire scrotum during walking

explanation: Spot on! Early on, it usually just feels like a painless, hard lump. That is why monthly self-checks are a lifesaver. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h5)

question: How do blood vessel (vascular) diseases lead to erectile dysfunction?

options.A: By causing excessive testosterone production in the testes
options.B: By blocking the normal production of seminal fluid
options.C: By destroying the nerves of the cremasteric muscle
options.D: By impairing adequate blood flow into the cavernous tissues

explanation: You got it! An erection needs good, healthy blood flow to fill the tissues. If vascular disease gets in the way, that flow is restricted. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is the primary test used to check sperm quality when investigating male infertility?

options.A: Prostate biopsy
options.B: Semen analysis
options.C: Scrotal ultrasound
options.D: Urodynamic testing

explanation: Awesome! A semen analysis looks at how many sperm there are, how well they swim (motility), and their shape. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is the best advice to give a young man on how to do a testicular self-exam?

options.A: Squeeze the epididymis firmly to check for inner fluid pockets
options.B: Perform the check monthly during or after a warm shower
options.C: Check the scrotum once a year during your annual medical exam
options.D: Examine the testicles only when experiencing lower back pain

explanation: Brilliant! Warm water relaxes the skin of the scrotum, making it much easier to feel around and notice any unusual lumps. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is the most critical nursing action for a patient with a continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) catheter after prostate surgery?

options.A: Removing the indwelling catheter immediately on postoperative day one
options.B: Restricting oral fluid intake to keep the drainage bag from filling
options.C: Clamping the catheter tube every hour to measure bladder capacity
options.D: Monitoring urine output color and clearing any clots to prevent blockage

explanation: You got it! CBI keeps blood clots from plugging up the catheter. As a nurse, watching the drainage color and keeping the lines clear prevents painful bladder spasms and blockages. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T11#GNS311_U1_T11_h7)

question: What gland releases follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone?

options.A: Posterior pituitary gland
options.B: Hypothalamus
options.C: Anterior pituitary gland
options.D: Adrenal cortex

explanation: The anterior pituitary gland responds to signals from the hypothalamus by secreting follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why does high prolactin stop a woman from releasing an egg during ovulation?

options.A: It blocks progesterone receptors in the uterus
options.B: It suppresses gonadotropin-releasing hormone
options.C: It destroys the developing ovarian follicles directly
options.D: It increases estrogen to dangerous levels

explanation: Extra prolactin gets in the way of brain signals, halting the hormone needed to trigger ovulation. It's a completely natural process, like how the body pauses cycles during breastfeeding! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h1)

question: What is the medical term for menstrual bleeding that is unusually heavy or lasts too long?

options.A: Metrorrhagia
options.B: Menorrhagia
options.C: Dysmenorrhea
options.D: Amenorrhea

explanation: Menorrhagia is the term for extra heavy or long periods. You will see this often in clinical practice when patients complain about soaking through pads too quickly. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which chemical messenger is mainly responsible for painful menstrual cramps?

options.A: Oxytocin
options.B: Prolactin
options.C: Prostaglandins
options.D: Estrogen

explanation: Prostaglandins make the muscles of the uterus contract strongly during your period. Higher levels mean stronger, more painful cramps! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h2)

question: What type of tissue makes up uterine fibroids?

options.A: Stratified squamous tissue
options.B: Glandular epithelial tissue
options.C: Adipose and fibrous tissue
options.D: Smooth muscle and connective tissue

explanation: Fibroids are non-cancerous growths made of the exact same smooth muscle and connective tissue found in the muscular wall of the uterus. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h3)

question: How is adenomyosis different from a normal uterus?

options.A: Endometrial tissue grows inside the muscular myometrium wall
options.B: The inner lining sheds continuously without hormonal triggers
options.C: Benign fibrous tumors develop on the outer serosal surface
options.D: The entire uterus drops below the pelvic floor muscles

explanation: Think of adenomyosis as the inner lining tissue burrowing into the middle muscle layer of the uterus, making the organ swell and feel tender. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h3)

question: What causes a follicular ovarian cyst to form?

options.A: The corpus luteum seals over and traps fluid inside
options.B: A benign tumor grows from surface epithelial cells
options.C: Endometrial cells attach to the outer surface of the ovary
options.D: A follicle fails to rupture and release an egg

explanation: Sometimes a fluid-filled egg sac just forgets to pop open and release its egg during ovulation. Instead, it keeps growing larger as a simple cyst! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h4)

question: A young woman comes to the clinic with sudden, severe pain on one side of her lower abdomen and vomiting. What condition should the nurse think of first?

options.A: Polycystic ovary syndrome
options.B: Follicular cyst rupture
options.C: Ovarian torsion
options.D: Endometriosis flare-up

explanation: Sudden one-sided pain and vomiting are classic red flags for ovarian torsion, where the ovary twists and cuts off its own blood supply. It's a true emergency! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h4)

question: Which two common sexually transmitted bacteria are most often linked to pelvic inflammatory disease?

options.A: Candida albicans and Trichomonas vaginalis
options.B: Human papillomavirus and Herpes simplex
options.C: Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus
options.D: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae

explanation: Chlamydia and gonorrhea are the troublemakers here. They love to travel upward from the vagina into the upper reproductive tract and cause infection. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h5)

question: Why does pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) raise a woman's risk of having an ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Hormonal imbalances stop the uterine lining from growing
options.B: Scar tissue blocks and damages the fallopian tubes
options.C: Infection prevents the ovaries from releasing eggs
options.D: Bacteria destroy the muscular walls of the uterus

explanation: When PID heals, it leaves behind scar tissue that narrows the tubes. If a fertilized egg gets stuck in that narrow, scarred tube, it implants right there instead of the uterus. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h5)

question: What is the most widely accepted theory for how endometrial tissue ends up outside the uterus?

options.A: Retrograde menstruation
options.B: Lymphatic vessel spread
options.C: Bacterial contamination
options.D: Direct muscular invasion

explanation: Retrograde menstruation means some menstrual flow travels backward through the fallopian tubes, carrying healthy uterine lining cells out into the pelvic cavity. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h6)

question: Why do misplaced endometrial implants cause ongoing pain and scarring in the pelvis?

options.A: They grow rapidly into malignant tumors within weeks
options.B: They release massive amounts of male hormones into the abdomen
options.C: They bleed during each cycle, causing local inflammation and adhesions
options.D: They destroy the nerves supplying the lower abdominal wall

explanation: Wherever these misplaced cells land, they still respond to monthly hormones by trying to 'bleed'. This trapped blood irritates nearby tissue, causing painful inflammation and sticky scar tissue. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which infection is most directly linked to the development of cervical cancer?

options.A: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
options.B: Human papillomavirus
options.C: Chlamydia trachomatis
options.D: Human immunodeficiency virus

explanation: High-risk strains of human papillomavirus (HPV) can hang around in the cells of the cervix for years and eventually cause cell changes that lead to cancer. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h7)

question: What is often the earliest warning sign of endometrial cancer in women who have gone through menopause?

options.A: Abnormal vaginal bleeding
options.B: Severe lower back pain
options.C: Rapid weight gain
options.D: Swollen lower extremities

explanation: Any spotting or bleeding after menopause is never normal and is usually the very first clue that prompts doctors to check the uterine lining. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h7)

question: What is the most important screening test nurses should encourage to catch early cell changes on the cervix?

options.A: Transvaginal ultrasound
options.B: Pap smear
options.C: CA-125 blood test
options.D: Endometrial biopsy

explanation: The Pap smear is a simple, life-saving screening tool that lets us spot weird cellular changes on the cervix long before they ever turn into cancer. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h8)

question: A patient who had severe pelvic inflammatory disease asks if she can still have children. What is the best way for a nurse to respond?

options.A: Assure her that past pelvic infections have no long-term impact on future reproductive health
options.B: Inform her that tube scarring can increase the risk of fertility challenges or ectopic pregnancy
options.C: Advise her to avoid getting pregnant because infections cause permanent sterility
options.D: Tell her that surgery can easily reverse any internal scarring caused by bacterial infections

explanation: Be honest yet supportive! Tube scarring can make getting pregnant trickier and raises ectopic risks, but it doesn't mean pregnancy is completely impossible. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T12#GNS311_U1_T12_h8)

question: Which hormone is produced by the Leydig cells in the testes?

options.A: Testosterone
options.B: Estrogen
options.C: Prolactin
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Great job! The Leydig cells are responsible for making testosterone, which is the main male sex hormone. You've got this! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T13#GNS311_U1_T13_h1)

question: What is the main job of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) in males?

options.A: Supporting sperm production in the Sertoli cells
options.B: Producing secondary sex characteristics in muscle
options.C: Triggering the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone
options.D: Controlling the contraction of the prostate gland

explanation: FSH works directly on the Sertoli cells in the testes to help nourish and build healthy sperm cells. Keep up the great studying! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T13#GNS311_U1_T13_h1)

question: Why is testicular torsion treated as an urgent medical emergency?

options.A: It causes an immediate permanent drop in total body testosterone
options.B: It always spreads a severe bacterial infection to the bladder
options.C: It triggers rapid enlargement of the prostate gland
options.D: It cuts off blood supply and can damage the tissue

explanation: When the spermatic cord twists, it blocks blood flow to the testicle. This is an emergency because the tissue needs oxygen fast to prevent permanent damage! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T13#GNS311_U1_T13_h2)

question: A young man comes to the clinic with sudden, severe pain in one side of his scrotum, and the testicle appears unusually high. What is the most likely issue?

options.A: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
options.B: Chronic epididymitis
options.C: Testicular torsion
options.D: Hydrocele formation

explanation: Sudden, severe scrotal pain with a high-riding testicle is the classic red flag for testicular torsion. Always watch out for this in clinical practice! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T13#GNS311_U1_T13_h2)

question: In which part of the prostate gland does benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) usually start?

options.A: Transition zone
options.B: Seminal vesicle
options.C: Central zone
options.D: Peripheral zone

explanation: BPH mostly starts in the inner transition zone, which wraps tightly around the urethra. That's why it quickly causes trouble with passing urine. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T13#GNS311_U1_T13_h3)

question: How does benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) cause urinary symptoms in older men?

options.A: By increasing the total daily production of urine
options.B: By stopping the bladder muscle from ever contracting
options.C: By squeezing the urethra and blocking urine flow
options.D: By destroying the nephrons in both kidneys

explanation: As the prostate grows larger, it presses against the urethra like a clamp, making it harder for urine to flow out smoothly. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T13#GNS311_U1_T13_h3)

question: What is the medical term for a testicle that fails to move down into the scrotum?

options.A: Cryptorchidism
options.B: Hypospadias
options.C: Phimosis
options.D: Hydrocele

explanation: Cryptorchidism simply means the testicle didn't make the normal journey down into the scrotum before birth. You are doing great mastering these terms! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T13#GNS311_U1_T13_h4)

question: Why does an undescended testicle have a higher risk of developing cancer later in life?

options.A: Constant friction against the pelvic bones triggers rapid cell division
options.B: The lack of hormones from the pituitary gland causes cell mutation
options.C: Blood flow to the testicle is normally twice as high in the abdomen
options.D: Higher body heat inside the abdomen damages the cells over time

explanation: The scrotum is naturally cooler, which sperm cells love. The warmer temperature inside the abdomen can harm these cells over time and raise cancer risks. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T13#GNS311_U1_T13_h4)

question: Which genetic condition with an extra X chromosome is a common cause of low testosterone and infertility in men?

options.A: Turner syndrome
options.B: Down syndrome
options.C: Klinefelter syndrome
options.D: Cystic fibrosis

explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY) affects testosterone production and sperm development. You're building a solid foundation in pathophysiology! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T13#GNS311_U1_T13_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a blockage-related (post-testicular) cause of male infertility?

options.A: Blocked vas deferens
options.B: Congenital absence of the sperm ducts
options.C: Epididymal scarring from infection
options.D: Klinefelter syndrome

explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is a chromosomal condition affecting the testes, whereas the other options are physical blockages in the tubes that carry sperm. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T13#GNS311_U1_T13_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of doing a routine semen analysis?

options.A: To check sperm count, movement, and shape
options.B: To measure the exact level of circulating testosterone
options.C: To check for malignant cells originating in the testes
options.D: To screen for active bacterial prostate infections

explanation: A semen analysis looks closely at the number, motility (movement), and morphology (shape) of sperm to check male fertility. Simple and straightforward! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T13#GNS311_U1_T13_h6)

question: A doctor wants to know if a patient's low testosterone is due to a problem in the testes or the pituitary gland. Which test helps figure this out?

options.A: Serum LH and FSH hormone levels
options.B: A prostate-specific antigen blood test
options.C: A complete blood count with differential
options.D: A routine urinalysis and urine culture

explanation: Checking LH and FSH levels from the pituitary gland helps doctors see if the issue starts in the brain (pituitary) or down in the testes. Excellent clinical thinking! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T13#GNS311_U1_T13_h6)

question: Why do nurses use the nursing process in patient care?

options.A: To speed up hospital discharge procedures
options.B: To provide a structured framework for delivering individualized care
options.C: To replace the need for direct communication with physicians
options.D: To diagnose complex medical diseases independently

explanation: Spot on! The nursing process helps you organize patient care into clear, step-by-step actions tailored to each person's unique needs. You've got this! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why is reproductive health nursing considered a sensitive area of care?

options.A: It involves more paperwork than other clinical departments
options.B: It deals with deeply personal aspects tied to self-image and culture
options.C: Medical treatments for these conditions are always experimental
options.D: Patients are rarely willing to talk about their symptoms

explanation: Exactly! Reproductive health touches on private parts of life, culture, and identity. Showing extra empathy and privacy goes a long way. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h1)

question: When taking a baseline reproductive health history, what should you include?

options.A: Childhood vaccination records
options.B: Daily dietary calorie and sodium intake
options.C: Menstrual patterns and obstetric history
options.D: Family history of cardiovascular disease only

explanation: Great job! A good reproductive history focuses on menstrual cycles, past pregnancies, and sexual health to understand the patient's baseline. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h2)

question: What is the best way to ask a patient about sensitive reproductive topics?

options.A: Asking rapidly to get through the uncomfortable questions quickly
options.B: Only asking if the patient brings up the topic first
options.C: Leaving the questions blank on the form for the doctor to handle
options.D: Building trust first to encourage honest and open sharing

explanation: Well done! Patients can feel shy or worried. Building a warm, non-judgmental space helps them open up so you can give the best care. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h2)

question: Which of these is a common nursing diagnosis for a patient dealing with a reproductive disorder?

options.A: Ineffective tissue perfusion related to cardiac arrest
options.B: Excess fluid volume related to renal failure
options.C: Disturbed body image related to surgical alterations
options.D: Impaired gas exchange related to airway collapse

explanation: Spot on! Surgeries or issues involving reproductive organs can deeply affect how patients see themselves, making body image a key focus. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h3)

question: What is the main reason for writing a nursing diagnosis in a patient care plan?

options.A: To determine the total cost of hospital treatment
options.B: To replace the medical diagnosis given by the physician
options.C: To legally clear the nurse from liability
options.D: To guide the selection of appropriate nursing interventions

explanation: Correct! A nursing diagnosis highlights how the patient is responding to a health issue, which helps you decide what nursing actions to take next. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h3)

question: What makes a patient outcome goal measurable in a care plan?

options.A: It includes specific criteria like pain scores or timeline targets
options.B: It is written only by the attending physician
options.C: It states that the patient will feel better eventually
options.D: It relies entirely on the nurse's personal opinion

explanation: You got it! Measurable goals use clear indicators—like a specific pain scale number or a timeframe—so you can easily tell if the patient is improving. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h4)

question: A patient is worried about her changing body after a hysterectomy. Which goal fits best in her care plan?

options.A: The patient will completely forget her anxiety within two hours
options.B: The nurse will make all decisions regarding her emotional care
options.C: The patient will verbalize feelings about body image changes before discharge
options.D: The patient will refuse to discuss her surgery with anyone

explanation: Brilliant! This goal is realistic, supportive, and lets the patient safely express her emotions regarding surgery. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h4)

question: What is a top nursing priority right after a reproductive surgery like a hysterectomy?

options.A: Restricting all fluid intake for the first 48 hours
options.B: Monitoring vital signs closely for signs of hemorrhage or infection
options.C: Preventing the patient from moving or walking for a week
options.D: Discharging the patient immediately to free up hospital beds

explanation: Spot on! Right after surgery, keeping a close eye on vitals helps you catch early warning signs of bleeding or infection. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h5)

question: Why do we encourage patients to get up and walk early after pelvic or reproductive surgery?

options.A: To speed up the patient's discharge paperwork
options.B: To eliminate the need for any pain medication
options.C: To ensure the surgical wound heals overnight
options.D: To prevent deep vein thrombosis and promote circulation

explanation: Correct! Early walking gets the blood moving in the legs, which protects our patients from dangerous blood clots. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h5)

question: What critical warning sign must you teach a patient who is taking hormonal reproductive medications?

options.A: Temporary fatigue in the evening
options.B: Sudden chest pain or leg swelling
options.C: Mild changes in hair texture
options.D: Slight increase in daily appetite

explanation: You nailed it! Hormones can raise the risk of blood clots, so chest pain or a swollen leg are major red flags patients must report immediately. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h6)

question: How can you make sure your patient truly understands a new reproductive medication?

options.A: By assuming the pharmacist already covered everything needed
options.B: By handing the patient a technical textbook to read alone
options.C: By focusing only on how much the prescription costs
options.D: By explaining expected benefits, side effects, and warning signs clearly

explanation: Exactly! Taking time to explain how the drug works and what side effects to watch for helps your patient stay safe and confident. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h6)

question: Which action shows the best emotional support for a patient dealing with infertility?

options.A: Telling the patient to stop worrying because everything happens for a reason
options.B: Listening actively and validating the patient's emotional grief
options.C: Avoiding the topic of children during all health conversations
options.D: Focusing solely on physical medication administration schedules

explanation: Well done! Infertility brings deep emotional pain. Listening without judgment helps patients process their grief in a safe space. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h7)

question: When should you refer a reproductive health patient to a specialist counselor?

options.A: When emotional distress exceeds basic supportive nursing care
options.B: Whenever the patient asks what medication they are taking
options.C: Only after the patient has completed all surgical treatments
options.D: Before the nurse performs any physical assessment

explanation: Spot on! While you provide great initial comfort, deep or complex emotional distress is best handled by mental health specialists. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h7)

question: What is the main focus during the evaluation phase of the nursing process?

options.A: Gathering baseline lab results before surgery
options.B: Determining whether the patient has achieved the expected care goals
options.C: Writing the initial health history admission paperwork
options.D: Deciding which medication to prescribe next without a doctor

explanation: Correct! Evaluation is all about checking back: did the patient reach the goals you set together during planning? [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h8)

question: Why is teaching patients preventive self-care so crucial before they leave the hospital?

options.A: To replace the need for any follow-up appointments
options.B: To make the discharge process take longer than necessary
options.C: To reduce the risk of recurring disorders and long-term complications
options.D: To ensure the patient never takes prescription drugs again

explanation: You got it! Good discharge teaching empowers patients to watch for warning signs and maintain their health at home. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T14#GNS311_U1_T14_h8)

question: What is the primary cause of hereditary conditions?

options.A: Exposure to common bacterial infections
options.B: Changes in the DNA sequence
options.C: Inadequate nutrition during pregnancy
options.D: Poor personal hygiene during childhood

explanation: Hereditary conditions stem directly from genetic mutations or alterations passed down from parents to their offspring. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h1)

question: Why is early identification of genetic risks important for nurses in primary healthcare?

options.A: It prevents patients from developing infectious diseases
options.B: It allows for proactive education and early risk reduction
options.C: It completely cures the genetic condition before birth
options.D: It eliminates the need for any further medical testing

explanation: Spotting risks early gives healthcare providers the chance to guide families and prevent severe complications before symptoms appear. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h1)

question: How many copies of a mutated gene must a child inherit to show symptoms of an autosomal recessive condition?

options.A: Two copies, one from each parent
options.B: Only one copy from the father
options.C: Four copies from extended family
options.D: Only one copy from the mother

explanation: Autosomal recessive disorders require both parents to pass on a copy of the altered gene for the child to be affected. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h2)

question: Why are males more commonly affected by X-linked recessive disorders than females?

options.A: The Y chromosome protects female offspring
options.B: Males possess only one X chromosome
options.C: X chromosomes only exist in male bodies
options.D: Females do not have any chromosomes

explanation: Since males only have one X chromosome, a single recessive mutation on that chromosome will express the disease, whereas females have a backup X chromosome. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h2)

question: What is the minimum number of generations a nurse should typically explore when taking a family health history?

options.A: Five generations
options.B: Only one generation
options.C: Three generations
options.D: Ten generations

explanation: Looking back across three generations (parents, children, and grandparents) helps reveal hidden inheritance patterns of hereditary conditions. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h3)

question: A young couple visits the clinic and mentions that multiple relatives on both sides died young from the same rare heart condition. What should the nurse do next?

options.A: Prescribe blood pressure medication for both partners
options.B: Construct a pedigree chart and refer them for genetic assessment
options.C: Advise them to change their cooking oil immediately
options.D: Tell them not to worry because heart disease is completely normal

explanation: A pattern of early-onset disease in multiple relatives is a major red flag requiring formal genetic risk evaluation. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h3)

question: What is the primary benefit of pre-conception genetic screening?

options.A: It allows couples to know their carrier status before pregnancy
options.B: It replaces the need for standard antenatal care
options.C: It immediately cures any existing genetic mutations
options.D: It guarantees that a child will never fall sick

explanation: Pre-conception screening reveals if partners carry matching recessive genes, helping them make informed family planning decisions. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h4)

question: Which of the following describes a key difference between screening tests and diagnostic tests in prenatal care?

options.A: Screening tests estimate risk, while diagnostic tests confirm a condition
options.B: Diagnostic tests are performed on every single pregnant woman
options.C: Screening tests are only done after birth
options.D: Screening tests use surgery, while diagnostic tests are painless

explanation: Screening tests only show the probability or risk of a disorder, whereas diagnostic tests provide a definitive diagnosis. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h4)

question: What is the teach-back method used for during patient education?

options.A: Writing prescription notes for the pharmacist
options.B: Asking the patient to explain the information back in their own words
options.C: Having the nurse read the textbook out loud to the patient
options.D: Testing the nurse's ability to memorize medical terminology

explanation: The teach-back method checks whether the patient truly understood the instructions by having them repeat the information. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h5)

question: Why must a nurse maintain neutrality when counseling patients about genetic risks?

options.A: To allow patients to make their own choices based on personal values
options.B: To prevent patients from asking questions about their family
options.C: To prove that genetics has no real impact on health
options.D: To ensure the hospital avoids paying for laboratory tests

explanation: Reproductive decisions are deeply personal; nurses must guide without imposing personal beliefs or forcing specific choices. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT an ethical responsibility of the nurse regarding genetic test results?

options.A: Providing accurate and non-judgmental information
options.B: Respecting the autonomy of the patient in decision-making
options.C: Sharing the results openly with extended family members without consent
options.D: Maintaining strict patient confidentiality to prevent discrimination

explanation: Nurses must protect patient privacy and confidentiality; sharing genetic results without explicit consent violates ethical standards. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h6)

question: How should a nurse handle cultural beliefs that attribute hereditary conditions solely to spiritual curses?

options.A: Publicly ridicule the family for holding traditional beliefs
options.B: Refuse to treat patients who mention spiritual explanations
options.C: Agree with the curse theory to avoid arguing with patients
options.D: Provide gentle, respectful education while addressing community myths

explanation: Nurses can bridge traditional beliefs and medical science through respectful education and community sensitization rather than harsh judgment. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h6)

question: Who typically acts as the central coordinator connecting various specialists and the patient in clinical settings?

options.A: The hospital accountant
options.B: The facility security guard
options.C: The pharmaceutical supplier
options.D: The nurse

explanation: Nurses coordinate care pathways, schedule referrals, and bridge communication between patients and the multidisciplinary healthcare team. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h7)

question: Why is a multidisciplinary team necessary for managing hereditary conditions?

options.A: It removes the need for nurses to speak directly with patients
options.B: Hospital regulations require at least ten staff members for every patient
options.C: No single profession has all the skills needed to address complex genetic and social needs
options.D: It ensures that laboratory scientists make all final clinical decisions

explanation: Hereditary conditions involve medical, emotional, and social challenges that require diverse expertise from multiple healthcare professionals. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T15#GNS311_U1_T15_h7)

question: What is the collective term for all the external structures of the female reproductive system?

options.A: Vestibule
options.B: Vulva
options.C: Perineum
options.D: Introitus

explanation: The vulva is the medical term used to describe all the external female genital structures combined. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why must a nurse know the exact landmarks of the vulva?

options.A: To pass a urinary catheter without missing the urethra
options.B: To prevent ovarian cysts
options.C: To measure blood pressure correctly
options.D: To track the exact day of ovulation

explanation: Spot on! Knowing your anatomy keeps procedures safe and stops you from accidentally placing a catheter into the vaginal opening instead of the urethra. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which layer of the uterus is primarily responsible for contractions during childbirth?

options.A: Myometrium
options.B: Perimetrium
options.C: Epimetrium
options.D: Endometrium

explanation: The myometrium is made of thick smooth muscle that contracts forcefully to push the baby out during labor. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h2)

question: What is the main job of the rugae inside the vaginal canal?

options.A: To constantly secrete lubricating hormones
options.B: To let the vagina stretch wide during childbirth
options.C: To trap bacteria and stop infections
options.D: To produce the monthly period blood

explanation: Well done! Those little folds (rugae) act like an accordion, giving extra tissue so the vagina can safely stretch during delivery. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h2)

question: Where does fertilization of an egg by a sperm normally happen?

options.A: Uterine cavity
options.B: Surface of the ovary
options.C: Fallopian tube
options.D: Vaginal canal

explanation: Correct! The sperm and egg usually meet and fuse right there in the fallopian tube on their journey. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h3)

question: What is the role of the fimbriae at the end of the fallopian tubes?

options.A: To sweep over the ovary and catch the released egg
options.B: To push sperm upward into the uterine cavity
options.C: To attach the ovary firmly to the pelvic wall
options.D: To secrete hormones that trigger monthly ovulation

explanation: The finger-like fimbriae use gentle sweeping movements to guide the newly released egg into the fallopian tube. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which hormone surge directly triggers ovulation around day 14 of the cycle?

options.A: Progesterone
options.B: Luteinizing hormone
options.C: Follicle-stimulating hormone
options.D: Human chorionic gonadotropin

explanation: You nailed it! A sudden spike in luteinizing hormone (LH) is the green light that causes the ovary to release a mature egg. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h4)

question: What causes the uterine lining to shed at the start of a new menstrual cycle?

options.A: A sharp drop in estrogen and progesterone
options.B: A sudden spike in body temperature
options.C: Implantation of a fertilized egg
options.D: The direct action of FSH

explanation: That is correct! When pregnancy doesn't happen, hormone levels drop, telling the body it's time to shed the lining during menstruation. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h4)

question: What hormone directly stimulates the initial growth and maturation of ovarian follicles?

options.A: Oxytocin
options.B: Prolactin
options.C: Testosterone
options.D: Follicle-stimulating hormone

explanation: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) is released by the pituitary gland to stimulate ovarian follicles to grow. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h5)

question: What happens to the follicular cells left behind in the ovary after ovulation?

options.A: They turn into permanent scar tissue
options.B: They turn into the corpus luteum and make progesterone
options.C: They travel down to meet the egg
options.D: They immediately dissolve and leave the pelvis

explanation: Spot on! The empty follicle gets a makeover into the corpus luteum, pumping out progesterone to get the uterus ready for a possible pregnancy. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h5)

question: How is menopause officially diagnosed in a patient?

options.A: Surgical removal of the fallopian tubes
options.B: A sudden spike in body temperature
options.C: Complete stop of pituitary hormones
options.D: Twelve straight months without a menstrual period

explanation: You got it! Clinicians look back and confirm menopause once a woman has gone a full 12 months without any bleeding. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h6)

question: Why do women often lose bone density after reaching menopause?

options.A: High FSH destroys the bone marrow
options.B: Lower estrogen levels remove the protective effect on bones
options.C: The uterus stops making calcium
options.D: Lack of progesterone stops water absorption

explanation: Correct! Estrogen helps keep bones strong, so when it drops after menopause, the risk of weak bones (osteoporosis) goes up. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h6)

question: What does the abbreviation LMP stand for in nursing assessments?

options.A: Last menstrual period
options.B: Luteal menstrual phase
options.C: Low mucosal pressure
options.D: Latest medical procedure

explanation: Easy and essential! LMP means Last Menstrual Period—a super important detail you will ask almost every female patient. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h7)

question: A patient comes to the clinic with severe lower belly pain and irregular bleeding. What is the best first nursing action?

options.A: Take a detailed menstrual history, including her last period date
options.B: Prepare her for immediate surgery
options.C: Tell the patient menopause has started
options.D: Advise her to stop all physical activity

explanation: Brilliant! Always start with a thorough history. Knowing her menstrual pattern helps the team figure out what might be going wrong. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T2#GNS311_U1_T2_h7)

question: What is the very first thing you should do when starting a reproductive health chat with a patient?

options.A: Document the patient's exact insurance details
options.B: Ensure physical privacy and a quiet environment
options.C: Review previous laboratory blood test results
options.D: Immediately perform a full physical pelvic exam

explanation: You've got this! Patients need a private, safe space to feel comfortable discussing sensitive topics. Always secure a quiet, private spot first before diving into personal health questions. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why is building trust so important during a reproductive health check-in?

options.A: It prevents the patient from asking questions about treatment costs
options.B: It encourages the patient to share sensitive personal information honestly
options.C: It guarantees the patient will accept all prescribed medications
options.D: It replaces the need for a detailed physical examination

explanation: Great nursing care starts with a good relationship! When patients trust you, they feel safe sharing personal details about their sexual or menstrual health without fear of judgment. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why do nurses always ask for a patient's age during a reproductive health history?

options.A: It is the only factor that determines their legal identity
options.B: It helps spot life-stage specific changes like puberty or menopause
options.C: It measures their overall physical height and weight
options.D: It dictates the exact type of insurance they must carry

explanation: Simple and straightforward! Age gives you quick clues about what life stage a patient is in, from teenage developmental questions to hormonal shifts later in life. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h2)

question: A patient works in a chemical factory and is worried about fertility. Which background detail helps you catch this risk?

options.A: Religious affiliation
options.B: Home address
options.C: Occupation
options.D: Marital status

explanation: Spot on! Knowing what a patient does for a living helps you check if they are exposed to workplace toxins or heavy physical stress that could affect their reproductive health. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the medical word for excessively heavy or long menstrual periods?

options.A: Menorrhagia
options.B: Amenorrhea
options.C: Dysmenorrhea
options.D: Menarche

explanation: You can remember this easily: 'Menorrhagia' means very heavy monthly flow that gets in the way of a woman's daily life and comfort. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h3)

question: Why is knowing the exact date of a patient's last menstrual period (LMP) so important?

options.A: It proves the patient has reached full menopause
options.B: It establishes a baseline for dating a pregnancy or spotting cycle changes
options.C: It indicates the exact day ovulation will occur next month
options.D: It measures the total amount of iron stored in the blood

explanation: You will use this all the time in clinic! The LMP helps us calculate expected due dates for pregnant mums and spot any unusual bleeding patterns early. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h3)

question: In midwifery, what does the term 'gravidity' mean?

options.A: The number of surgical deliveries performed
options.B: The total number of times a woman has been pregnant
options.C: The number of children currently living at home
options.D: The total weight of all babies delivered

explanation: Think of gravidity as the pregnancy counter! It counts every single time a woman has been pregnant, no matter how the pregnancy ended. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h4)

question: A patient has delivered two full-term babies, had one early miscarriage, and has two living children. What is her parity?

options.A: Three
options.B: Four
options.C: Two
options.D: Five

explanation: You've got this! Parity counts pregnancies that made it past 20 weeks (viable births). Since she had two full-term deliveries, her parity is 2. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h4)

question: What is the medical term for pain felt during sexual intercourse?

options.A: Dysmenorrhea
options.B: Dyspareunia
options.C: Dysuria
options.D: Dystocia

explanation: Break it down: 'Dys-' means painful, and 'pareunia' relates to intercourse. It's a key symptom to ask about gently during health histories. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h5)

question: Why must nurses ask patients about their family planning or contraceptive methods?

options.A: To replace the need for asking about sexual partners
options.B: To judge the personal lifestyle choices of the patient
options.C: To evaluate pregnancy prevention methods and potential hormone side effects
options.D: To determine how much tax the patient pays

explanation: No judgment here—just good nursing! Asking about contraception helps us understand cycle changes, check for side effects, and support the patient's family goals. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which past surgery is most likely to cause scar tissue (adhesions) that could affect future fertility?

options.A: Pelvic surgery or surgery inside the lower belly
options.B: Appendectomy on the arm
options.C: Tonsillectomy
options.D: Knee arthroscopy

explanation: Surgeries close to the reproductive organs can leave behind small bands of scar tissue that might twist or block the fallopian tubes. Good to keep in mind! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h6)

question: How can an ongoing health condition like diabetes affect a woman's reproductive cycle?

options.A: It prevents the patient from ever taking oral medications
options.B: It completely stops a woman from ever reaching menopause
options.C: It causes immediate permanent vision loss in newborns
options.D: It can throw off hormone balance and lead to irregular periods

explanation: Diabetes affects the body's entire metabolic system, which can sometimes interfere with regular ovulation and cause irregular menstrual bleeding. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h6)

question: How can severe emotional stress or extreme physical exercise affect a woman's monthly cycle?

options.A: It can mess with brain signals and cause missed periods
options.B: It causes permanent cessation of all body hair
options.C: It doubles the daily production of red blood cells
options.D: It permanently enlarges the uterus

explanation: The brain and hormones are closely linked! High stress or over-exercising can trick the hypothalamus into pausing the hormones needed for regular ovulation. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h7)

question: Which lifestyle habit is crucial to screen for because it directly harms a developing baby during pregnancy?

options.A: Drinking filtered tap water
options.B: Eating green leafy vegetables
options.C: Using tobacco products
options.D: Walking thirty minutes daily

explanation: Tobacco smoke carries harmful toxins that cut down blood flow to the womb and pose serious risks to an unborn baby. Always a key lifestyle question! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h7)

question: During a reproductive review of systems, which symptom is a red flag that needs a closer look?

options.A: Eating three balanced meals every day
options.B: Unexplained abnormal vaginal discharge or odor
options.C: A normal resting heart rate
options.D: Sleeping eight hours every night

explanation: Unusual discharge or smells are often the body's way of signaling an infection or irritation in the reproductive tract that needs treatment. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h8)

question: A patient reports hot flashes, night sweats, and irregular cycles. Which body systems are these complaints linked to?

options.A: Endocrine and reproductive systems
options.B: Musculoskeletal system
options.C: Gastrointestinal system
options.D: Respiratory system

explanation: You've got this! Hot flashes and night sweats happen when estrogen levels shift, which ties directly back to our hormone (endocrine) and reproductive systems. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T3#GNS311_U1_T3_h8)

question: Why should a patient empty their bladder right before a pelvic examination?

options.A: To measure baseline kidney function accurately
options.B: To collect a routine 24-hour urine sample
options.C: To reduce pelvic discomfort and improve organ palpation
options.D: To prevent sudden drops in systemic blood pressure

explanation: Great job! An empty bladder sits lower down, making the exam much more comfortable for the patient and allowing you to feel the reproductive organs clearly. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why is it important for a nurse to explain each step before starting a reproductive assessment?

options.A: To distract the patient from physical pain
options.B: To decrease patient anxiety and build trust
options.C: To speed up the total time spent in the room
options.D: To fulfill strict legal billing requirements

explanation: Spot on! Reproductive exams can feel intimidating. Explaining what you are about to do calms nerves and helps the patient trust you. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which type of lubricant must you use during a pelvic exam if a Pap smear is planned?

options.A: Petroleum-based jelly
options.B: Water-soluble lubricant
options.C: Surgical mineral oil
options.D: Silicone-based oil

explanation: You got it! Petroleum or silicone jellies can mess up cellular lab samples like Pap smears. Always stick to water-soluble products. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h2)

question: Why must speculums be either single-use plastic or properly sterilized metal?

options.A: To prevent the transmission of infections between patients
options.B: To make the examination completely painless for everyone
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of hospital supplies
options.D: To ensure the equipment feels warm to the patient's touch

explanation: Spot on! Because these instruments touch mucous membranes, keeping them sterile or disposable stops bacteria and viruses from spreading from person to person. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h2)

question: Unexplained facial hair growth in a female patient can be a sign of which condition?

options.A: Chronic kidney disease
options.B: Polycystic ovary syndrome
options.C: Iron deficiency anemia
options.D: Essential hypertension

explanation: Correct! Extra facial hair (hirsutism) is often linked to higher androgen levels, which are common in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h3)

question: A male patient has enlarged breast tissue during a routine check. Which body system is likely involved?

options.A: The musculoskeletal system
options.B: The urinary system
options.C: The endocrine system
options.D: The integumentary system

explanation: You nailed it! Gynecomastia (enlarged male breast tissue) is usually driven by hormone imbalances, which fall under the endocrine system. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h3)

question: What position is a female patient usually placed in for a full pelvic examination?

options.A: Prone position
options.B: Trendelenburg position
options.C: Semi-Fowler position
options.D: Lithotomy position

explanation: Correct! The lithotomy position (lying on the back with legs in stirrups) gives you the best view and access for checking pelvic organs. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the main goal of bimanual palpation during a female pelvic exam?

options.A: To check for external skin lesions on the labia majora
options.B: To collect a sample of surface cells from the outer surface of the cervix
options.C: To measure the exact pH balance of vaginal fluid secretions
options.D: To evaluate the size, shape, and consistency of internal organs like the uterus

explanation: Spot on! By placing one hand inside the vagina and the other on the lower belly, you can 'sandwich' the organs to feel their size and tenderness. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h4)

question: Which structures should you palpate when doing a routine male genital check?

options.A: Testes and epididymis
options.B: Bulbourethral glands only
options.C: Ureters and renal pelvis
options.D: Seminal vesicles and bladder

explanation: You got it! Gently checking the testes and the epididymis helps you spot any lumps, swelling, or tenderness early on. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h5)

question: Why is teaching self-examination important in male reproductive care?

options.A: It is the only reliable way to diagnose a urinary tract infection
options.B: It replaces the need for any future professional medical visits
options.C: It helps patients detect early changes like lumps or swelling
options.D: It prevents the normal age-related decrease in testosterone

explanation: Correct! Self-exams empower patients to notice small changes right away, leading to quicker medical help and better health results. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of doing a routine Pap smear?

options.A: To screen for precancerous cellular changes on the cervix
options.B: To diagnose a severe bacterial urinary tract infection
options.C: To measure circulating levels of reproductive hormones
options.D: To test for active yeast infections in the vagina

explanation: Spot on! A Pap smear collects cervical cells to look for unusual changes before they have a chance to turn into cervical cancer. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which mistake during a cervical swab can ruin the lab result?

options.A: Explaining the testing procedure to the patient too early
options.B: Using a plastic speculum instead of a cold metal one
options.C: Allowing the patient to empty their bladder before the exam
options.D: Leaving excess mucus on the cervix before taking the sample

explanation: You got it! Too much mucus or discharge blocks the cells, making it impossible for the lab tech to read the sample accurately. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which of these is a good example of objective documentation during a reproductive assessment?

options.A: Patient seems overly anxious and does not like pelvic exams
options.B: Skin intact, no lesions or abnormal discharge noted on the labia
options.C: Patient is probably hiding symptoms due to personal embarrassment
options.D: External genitalia look completely normal and healthy overall

explanation: Spot on! Objective notes focus on clear, observable facts rather than personal guesses or vague opinions. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h7)

question: Why should nurses avoid using vague words like 'normal' when charting physical assessments?

options.A: It violates patient privacy laws to write short descriptive sentences
options.B: Patients have a legal right to erase that word from their records
options.C: Hospital computers will automatically reject entries containing that word
options.D: Different healthcare workers can interpret vague words in different ways

explanation: Correct! Using clear, descriptive details ensures every nurse or doctor reading the chart has the exact same picture of the patient's condition. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T4#GNS311_U1_T4_h7)

question: Why do doctors order diagnostic tests in reproductive health?

options.A: To permanently cure all chronic reproductive tract infections
options.B: To replace the need for a physical clinical examination
options.C: To induce immediate menopause in older female patients
options.D: To investigate underlying structural or hormonal abnormalities

explanation: Spot on! Diagnostic tests help us figure out the root cause of any structural, hormonal, or functional issues in the reproductive system. You've got this! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T5#GNS311_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why does the timing of certain reproductive health tests matter so much?

options.A: Infection rates are highest right after ovulation occurs
options.B: Hospitals only have laboratory reagents available on specific days of the month
options.C: Patients are too weak to undergo procedures during the first week of bleeding
options.D: Hormone levels and uterine lining thickness change during the menstrual cycle

explanation: Exactly! Hormones and tissue structures shift naturally all month long, so tests need to be timed right to get accurate results. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T5#GNS311_U1_T5_h1)

question: What is the nurse's main role when it comes to informed consent?

options.A: Writing the medical prescription for the diagnostic procedure
options.B: Explaining the legal liability of the hospital to the family
options.C: Deciding whether the patient is well enough to undergo the test
options.D: Ensuring the patient understands the procedure and has signed voluntarily

explanation: Well done! The nurse makes sure the patient truly gets what the doctor explained and is agreeing of their own free will—no pressure! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T5#GNS311_U1_T5_h2)

question: Why is emotional and psychological support so important during reproductive workups?

options.A: Procedures often involve sensitive body parts and fears about fertility or disease
options.B: Anxiety prevents the laboratory from processing blood samples accurately
options.C: Patients are legally required to attend counseling before any pelvic exam
options.D: Physical pain cannot be managed with medication if the patient is stressed

explanation: Spot on. Reproductive organs carry deep emotional meaning, so it is totally normal for patients to feel anxious, embarrassed, or scared. Your warm support means everything! [learn more](GNS311_U1_T5#GNS311_U1_T5_h2)

question: In a regular 28-day cycle, when do we usually check serum progesterone to see if ovulation happened?

options.A: Mid-luteal phase around day 21
options.B: During active menstrual bleeding
options.C: Immediately at the end of menses
options.D: On the exact day of ovulation

explanation: You got it! Progesterone peaks after ovulation, making day 21 the sweet spot in a standard cycle to check if ovulation took place. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T5#GNS311_U1_T5_h3)

question: A male patient is getting a semen analysis for fertility checks. What should you tell him to do beforehand?

options.A: Avoid eating any protein-rich foods for 48 hours prior to the test
options.B: Keep the semen sample in a house refrigerator until arriving at the clinic
options.C: Collect the sample using ordinary household soap and water for hygiene
options.D: Maintain a period of sexual abstinence for 2 to 5 days before collection

explanation: Correct! A 2 to 5 day window of abstinence helps ensure the sperm count and movement are measured as accurately as possible. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T5#GNS311_U1_T5_h3)

question: Which imaging test uses a special dye to check if the Fallopian tubes are open?

options.A: Scrotal Doppler ultrasound
options.B: Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging
options.C: Hysterosalpingography
options.D: Transvaginal ultrasound

explanation: Brilliant! Hysterosalpingography involves putting dye into the uterus and taking X-rays to see if the fluid flows nicely through open Fallopian tubes. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T5#GNS311_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why might a doctor order a transvaginal ultrasound instead of a transabdominal one?

options.A: It allows visualization of the entire abdomen including the liver and stomach
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for any patient preparation or consent
options.C: It is completely painless and causes zero discomfort for all patients
options.D: It places the transducer closer to the pelvic organs for clearer images

explanation: Spot on! Slipping the probe into the vaginal canal brings it right next to the uterus and ovaries, giving us a much sharper picture than scanning through the tummy wall. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T5#GNS311_U1_T5_h4)

question: Which scope procedure lets the doctor look directly inside the uterine cavity?

options.A: Colposcopy
options.B: Hysteroscopy
options.C: Cystoscopy
options.D: Laparoscopy

explanation: You nailed it! A hysteroscopy uses a tiny scope passed through the cervix to check out the inside lining of the uterus. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T5#GNS311_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is the big win of using laparoscopy instead of traditional open surgery?

options.A: General anesthesia is never required during laparoscopic pelvic procedures
options.B: It provides a clear view of internal organs without needing any camera lights
options.C: Smaller incisions lead to faster physical recovery and less postoperative pain
options.D: Patients can leave the hospital immediately before the procedure even finishes

explanation: Correct! Tiny puncture holes mean less body trauma, quicker healing, and way less pain for the patient. [learn more](GNS311_U1_T5#GNS311_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is the main goal of a routine Pap smear?

options.A: Treating active pelvic inflammatory disease with local antiseptics
options.B: Screening for cervical cancer and precancerous cellular changes
options.C: Measuring exact progesterone and estrogen hormone levels in the blood
