options.B: Epistaxis from the nose
options.C: Petechiae on the skin
options.D: Gingival bleeding while brushing

explanation: Bleeding inside the skull (intracranial hemorrhage) puts heavy pressure on the brain. It can cause rapid confusion, unconsciousness, or worse if nurses don't catch it early. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h3)

question: Why might a patient with very low white blood cells (neutropenia) NOT show classic signs of infection like pus?

options.A: They lack enough white blood cells to mount an inflammatory response
options.B: Their body temperature stays too low to support white blood cell activity
options.C: Their platelets bind up all the available immune cells
options.D: Their blood vessels are too constricted to allow fluid movement

explanation: Pus is basically a pile of used white blood cells that fought an infection. If a patient doesn't have enough white blood cells to begin with, infections can sneak in quietly—often with just a fever as the only clue! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h4)

question: An oncology patient on chemotherapy develops a sudden fever of 38.8°C with no cough or sore spots. What should the nurse do right away?

options.A: Apply a warm compress to likely infection sites to check for tenderness
options.B: Encourage oral fluid intake and apply cold sponging to reduce the fever
options.C: Report the fever immediately and prepare for blood cultures and antibiotics
options.D: Recheck the temperature in four hours to see if it drops naturally

explanation: For a neutropenic patient, a fever is an emergency! Because they lack white blood cells to fight back, a small fever can turn into life-threatening sepsis very quickly. Always act fast. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h4)

question: How does the heart first try to make up for a severe lack of red blood cells (anemia)?

options.A: By decreasing the volume of plasma to thicken the blood
options.B: By increasing heart rate and cardiac output to circulate blood faster
options.C: By constricting peripheral blood vessels to raise blood pressure
options.D: By slowing down heart rate to let blood absorb more oxygen

explanation: Since each drop of blood is carrying less oxygen, the heart pumps faster and harder to keep enough oxygen moving around the body. It's working overtime! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h5)

question: What long-term heart problem often develops from chronic, untreated severe anemia?

options.A: Primary pulmonary hypertension
options.B: High-output heart failure
options.C: Chronic deep vein thrombosis
options.D: Peripheral artery disease

explanation: Imagine running a car engine at top speed every single day—eventually, it wears out. The heart muscle gets exhausted from constantly overworking to pump oxygen-poor blood, leading to heart failure. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h5)

question: Why do patients who receive repeated blood transfusions end up with an overload of iron in their bodies?

options.A: Transfused red blood cells immediately break down in the digestive tract
options.B: The human body lacks an active physiological mechanism to excrete excess iron
options.C: Kidneys filter out red blood cells but trap all the iron in the nephrons
options.D: The liver actively manufactures iron whenever foreign blood is introduced

explanation: Our bodies are great at holding onto iron, but we have no natural way to get rid of extra amounts. Every transfusion adds more iron, which builds up over time. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h6)

question: Which organs take the biggest hit from long-term iron overload caused by frequent blood transfusions?

options.A: Lungs, pleura, and upper airways
options.B: Brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves
options.C: Liver, heart, and endocrine glands
options.D: Stomach, intestines, and pancreas

explanation: Extra iron loves to settle down in hard-working organs like the liver, the heart muscle, and hormone-making glands, eventually causing tissue damage if not treated. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h6)

question: What is the main danger of polycythemia vera (a condition where the body makes too many blood cells)?

options.A: Hyperviscosity and abnormal clot formation
options.B: Massive platelet destruction and bleeding
options.C: Severe iron deficiency and rapid hemolysis
options.D: Total bone marrow aplasia and infection

explanation: When you have too many cells packed into the blood, it gets thick and sludgy (hyperviscosity). This makes dangerous blood clots much more likely to form. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h7)

question: A patient with a blood disorder that causes easy clotting suddenly complains of shortness of breath and sharp chest pain. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Acute chest syndrome
options.B: Splenic sequestration
options.C: Pulmonary embolism
options.D: High-output heart failure

explanation: Sharp chest pain and sudden breathlessness in a clot-prone patient are classic red flags for a pulmonary embolism—a clot traveling into the blood vessels of the lungs. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h7)

question: Which lab results are most important for a nurse to watch when caring for a patient with a bleeding disorder?

options.A: Liver enzymes and serum creatinine levels
options.B: Red blood cell count and serum iron levels
options.C: Platelet count and coagulation profiles
options.D: White blood cell differential and blood cultures

explanation: Platelet counts and clotting tests (like PT and APTT) show directly how well the patient's blood can form a clot and stop bleeding. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h8)

question: Which of these nursing actions is NOT a priority when caring for a patient having an acute sickle cell pain crisis?

options.A: Providing adequate hydration with intravenous fluids
options.B: Administering prescribed analgesics for pain relief
options.C: Administering supplemental oxygen if oxygen saturation is low
options.D: Administering scheduled doses of oral iron supplements

explanation: Iron pills won't help during a sickle cell crisis and could be harmful. The main goals during a crisis are keeping the patient well-hydrated, giving oxygen if needed, and managing their pain! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T14#GNS311_U2_T14_h8)

question: What is the main goal of primary prevention in haematology?

options.A: To manage chronic pain in sickle cell disease
options.B: To detect early signs of a bleeding disorder
options.C: To stop a blood disorder from ever developing
options.D: To cure a patient with advanced leukemia

explanation: Primary prevention focuses on stopping diseases before they start through healthy lifestyle habits and vaccinations. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h1)

question: Which nursing action is an example of secondary prevention for a blood disorder?

options.A: Educating the community about eating iron-rich foods
options.B: Screening routine complete blood counts for a pregnant woman
options.C: Administering a blood transfusion for severe hemorrhagic shock
options.D: Providing physical therapy for joint damage in hemophilia

explanation: Secondary prevention involves early detection and screening to catch conditions before they cause severe problems. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h1)

question: Which vitamin helps the body absorb plant-based iron much better?

options.A: Vitamin E
options.B: Vitamin D
options.C: Vitamin C
options.D: Vitamin K

explanation: Taking vitamin C alongside plant-based iron sources significantly improves how well the gut absorbs the mineral. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h2)

question: A patient with low iron levels eats plenty of beans and spinach. What advice should the nurse give to improve iron absorption?

options.A: Cook the vegetables in a microwave without water
options.B: Drink fresh orange juice or eat tomatoes with the meal
options.C: Drink a cup of strong black tea right after eating
options.D: Take the iron food with a glass of whole milk

explanation: Orange juice and tomatoes are rich in vitamin C, which enhances the absorption of non-heme iron found in plants. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h2)

question: Why are fresh flowers and live plants banned from the room of an immunocompromised patient?

options.A: They attract stinging insects into the hospital room
options.B: Their soil and standing water harbor dangerous fungi
options.C: Their strong scent can trigger severe allergic asthma
options.D: They consume too much oxygen in a closed space

explanation: Soil and stagnant water are breeding grounds for fungi and bacteria that can easily cause severe infections in patients with low white blood cells. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h3)

question: What is the primary reason for placing a patient with severe neutropenia on protective isolation?

options.A: To prevent them from leaving the ward before discharge
options.B: To keep their contagious blood disease away from others
options.C: To shield their fragile body from outside germs
options.D: To reduce the noise level around their hospital bed

explanation: Protective isolation protects a patient who lacks enough white blood cells to fight off everyday germs in the environment. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h3)

question: Which laboratory test is most commonly used as an initial screening tool for blood disorders?

options.A: Liver enzyme panel
options.B: Bone marrow biopsy
options.C: Complete blood count
options.D: Cerebral spinal fluid analysis

explanation: A complete blood count provides essential baseline values for red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a routine screening objective for inherited blood conditions in the community?

options.A: Providing immediate blood transfusions to healthy carriers
options.B: Raising public awareness about genetic counseling
options.C: Identifying carrier status before family planning
options.D: Detecting early signs of trait markers in newborns

explanation: Carriers of genetic blood traits are generally healthy and do not require blood transfusions. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h4)

question: Why is maintaining good hydration crucial for a patient with sickle cell disease?

options.A: It speeds up the breakdown of old iron deposits in the liver
options.B: It stops the bone marrow from producing abnormal platelets
options.C: It increases the total number of white blood cells in circulation
options.D: It keeps blood thin and prevents red blood cells from sickling

explanation: Dehydration concentrates the blood and causes red blood cells to warp and block vessels, so fluids help prevent painful crises. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h5)

question: A young adult with sickle cell disease is preparing for a mountain hiking trip. What is the most important warning the nurse should give?

options.A: Cold mountain water will permanently cure chronic joint inflammation
options.B: Low oxygen levels at high altitudes can trigger a painful sickling crisis
options.C: Hiking boots will cause severe foot ulcers due to poor circulation
options.D: Mountain air contains too many allergens that destroy red blood cells

explanation: High altitudes have lower oxygen levels, which can easily provoke red blood cells to change shape and block blood flow. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h5)

question: Which blood test is used to monitor the therapeutic level of the anticoagulant warfarin?

options.A: White blood cell differential
options.B: Fast blood glucose level
options.C: International Normalized Ratio
options.D: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate

explanation: The International Normalized Ratio measures how long it takes for a patient's blood to clot while taking warfarin. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h6)

question: A patient taking a daily anticoagulant medication reports finding dark, tarry stools. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: A normal reaction to eating green leafy vegetables
options.B: Rapid dehydration due to warm weather conditions
options.C: Bleeding somewhere in the upper gastrointestinal tract
options.D: An infection caused by low white blood cell counts

explanation: Dark, tarry stools indicate digested blood coming from the stomach or upper gut, which is a sign of bleeding caused by anticoagulants. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h6)

question: What is a major benefit of community genetic counseling for inherited blood disorders?

options.A: Manufacturing safe blood products for local hospital use
options.B: Providing free meals for patients with severe chronic anemia
options.C: Helping families understand their risk of passing conditions to children
options.D: Treating acute bleeding episodes in emergency rooms

explanation: Genetic counseling educates couples about their carrier status and the statistical chances of having children with conditions like sickle cell anemia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h7)

question: Why must nurses adjust their teaching style when educating patients about blood health?

options.A: To prove that modern medicine is superior to local traditions
options.B: To match the patient's literacy level and cultural background
options.C: To make the education session finish much faster
options.D: To ensure the medical terms are as complex as possible

explanation: Clear, culturally sensitive communication ensures patients truly understand how to protect their health and follow prevention guidelines. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T15#GNS311_U2_T15_h7)

question: Why do nurses take a detailed health history when assessing a patient's blood (haematological) health?

options.A: To calculate the exact financial cost of patient care
options.B: To catch subtle clues about blood and clotting abnormalities
options.C: To diagnose the exact type of cancer immediately
options.D: To replace the need for routine laboratory blood tests

explanation: Spotting early clues in a patient's history helps you catch blood and clotting issues before they become serious. Great job thinking like a nurse! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h1)

question: When a patient has a blood disorder, why must you check multiple body systems instead of just one area?

options.A: Haematological disorders only affect the skin and the muscles
options.B: Blood circulates throughout the entire body and impacts every organ
options.C: Blood cell counts change completely every single hour
options.D: Hospital protocols require checking every organ for all patients

explanation: Remember, blood travels everywhere! Because it touches every part of the body, a blood problem can show up as symptoms in different organs. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h1)

question: Sickle cell disease is most commonly found in people of which ancestral background?

options.A: African, Mediterranean, or Middle Eastern descent
options.B: Northern European and Scandinavian descent
options.C: East Asian and Pacific Islander descent
options.D: Indigenous Australian and New Zealand descent

explanation: Inherited conditions like sickle cell anaemia are much more common in specific ancestral groups from regions like Africa, the Mediterranean, and the Middle East. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h2)

question: A 65-year-old worker with long-term chemical exposure comes in with tiredness. Which background factor makes you suspect a blood issue?

options.A: The geographical location of the local grocery store
options.B: The patient's marital status and living arrangements
options.C: The patient's preferred method of daily transportation
options.D: Occupational chemical exposure linked to bone marrow problems

explanation: Workplace exposure to chemicals like benzene can damage the bone marrow and lead to blood issues over time. Always ask about your patients' jobs! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is a very common complaint you will hear from patients who have anaemia?

options.A: Chronic fatigue and shortness of breath
options.B: Uncontrolled involuntary muscle twitching
options.C: Sudden inability to move the left arm
options.D: Severe pain in the lower right abdomen

explanation: When red blood cells are low, they carry less oxygen. This leaves the body tissues starving for oxygen, causing constant tiredness and breathlessness. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why is it helpful to ask patients about the exact trigger and how long their bleeding episodes last?

options.A: It replaces the need to check the patient's blood pressure
options.B: It guarantees that the patient requires immediate surgery
options.C: It helps differentiate between platelet disorders and clotting factor deficiencies
options.D: It proves the patient is exaggerating their symptoms to the doctor

explanation: Different bleeding patterns give us great clues! They help us figure out if the issue is with sticky platelets or the proteins that help blood clot. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h3)

question: Which skin sign is most often seen in patients with a low platelet count (thrombocytopenia)?

options.A: Yellow discoloration of the skin
options.B: Severe dry and peeling patches
options.C: Petechiae and easy bruising
options.D: Widespread painful blistering

explanation: Without enough platelets to patch tiny leaks in blood vessels, patients easily get tiny red dots (petechiae) and bruises from minor bumps. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why might a patient with a severe vitamin B12 deficiency feel numbness or tingling in their hands and feet?

options.A: Vitamin B12 is essential for maintaining healthy nerve function
options.B: The patient is experiencing a sudden adverse reaction to food
options.C: Red blood cells press directly against the spinal cord
options.D: Low vitamins cause the blood vessels in the fingers to instantly shrink

explanation: Vitamin B12 doesn't just help blood—it keeps our nerves healthy too! When it's low, patients can feel tingling or numbness along with anaemia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why is chronic kidney disease an important thing to note when taking a patient's blood history?

options.A: It triggers sudden and uncontrollable blood clotting
options.B: Damaged kidneys produce less erythropoietin, causing anaemia
options.C: It causes the liver to stop storing iron completely
options.D: Kidney failure immediately destroys all white blood cells

explanation: Healthy kidneys make erythropoietin, the hormone that tells the bone marrow to build red blood cells. When kidneys fail, that hormone drops, leading to anaemia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is the main reason a nurse asks a patient about a family history of blood disorders?

options.A: To predict the exact date the patient will recover
options.B: To find out if family members can pay for hospital bills
options.C: To identify inherited conditions passed down through genes
options.D: To determine which hospital room the patient prefers

explanation: Conditions like haemophilia and sickle cell disease are passed down from parents to children through genes. Family history is a great shortcut to knowing what to look out for! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which of these substances can interfere with platelet function and raise a patient's risk of bleeding?

options.A: Inhaled medications for mild asthma
options.B: Prescribed eye drops for glaucoma
options.C: Herbal supplements like garlic and ginkgo
options.D: Standard daily multivitamins with calcium

explanation: Some common herbal supplements act like natural blood thinners. Always ask patients about herbs and supplements they take at home! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h6)

question: A patient scheduled for surgery takes daily aspirin for joint pain. What is your main concern as their nurse?

options.A: Aspirin causes a dangerous spike in white blood cell counts
options.B: Aspirin inhibits platelet function and can cause excessive bleeding
options.C: Aspirin turns the patient's blood bright green in the tubing
options.D: Aspirin completely stops the kidneys from producing urine

explanation: Aspirin stops platelets from sticking together properly. Before surgery, this puts the patient at high risk for heavy bleeding. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h6)

question: A strict vegan diet without any supplements puts a patient at higher risk for which type of nutritional anaemia?

options.A: Inherited sickle cell anaemia
options.B: Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia
options.C: Acute iron overload anaemia
options.D: Primary aplastic anaemia

explanation: Natural vitamin B12 is found mostly in animal products. Patients on a strict vegan diet need supplements or fortified foods to avoid getting B12 deficiency anaemia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h7)

question: Why should you ask a patient about their alcohol intake when doing a blood assessment?

options.A: Alcohol increases the body's ability to absorb extra iron
options.B: Alcohol completely cures most inherited bleeding disorders over time
options.C: Patients who drink alcohol never need laboratory blood work
options.D: Heavy alcohol use can suppress bone marrow and impair liver clotting factors

explanation: Heavy drinking slows down blood cell production in the bone marrow and damages the liver, which makes it harder to produce clotting proteins. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T2#GNS311_U2_T2_h7)

question: Why does a patient with severe anemia often have a fast heartbeat (tachycardia)?

options.A: The lungs stop absorbing carbon dioxide properly
options.B: Blood vessels become strictly constricted throughout the body
options.C: White blood cells are attacking the heart muscle tissue
options.D: The heart pumps faster to make up for low oxygen carrying capacity

explanation: When red blood cells are low, your body doesn't get enough oxygen. To help out, the heart beats faster to pump the remaining cells around the body quicker. You've got this! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why is general inspection a great first step before doing a physical exam on a patient with a blood disorder?

options.A: It provides a quick way to measure the exact red blood cell count
options.B: It replaces the need to check laboratory blood test results completely
options.C: It is the only legal way to diagnose leukemia in the ward
options.D: It helps spot immediate signs of distress, fatigue, and distress clues

explanation: Looking at your patient first gives you a quick overall picture of their energy level, comfort, and obvious physical symptoms before you dive into detailed touching and listening. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h1)

question: What tiny spots typically appear on a patient's skin when their platelet count is very low?

options.A: Jaundice
options.B: Koilonychia
options.C: Cyanosis
options.D: Petechiae

explanation: Petechiae are tiny, pinpoint red or purple spots that show up on the skin when platelets are too low to stop minor capillary leaks. Great to know for your clinicals! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h2)

question: A patient comes in with yellow eyes (sclera) and dark urine. What process is likely happening?

options.A: Sudden increase in blood clotting factors causing blockages
options.B: Dangerous drop in white blood cells leading to severe infection
options.C: Rapid breakdown of red blood cells releasing bilirubin
options.D: Severe lack of dietary iron causing spoon-shaped nails

explanation: Yellowing eyes and skin point to hemolysis—where red blood cells break down too fast, releasing excess bilirubin into the body. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the medical term for a smooth, red, and painful tongue linked to nutritional shortages?

options.A: Petechiae
options.B: Glossitis
options.C: Epistaxis
options.D: Jaundice

explanation: Glossitis just means inflammation of the tongue. It makes the tongue look smooth and red, and you'll often see it in patients with vitamin B12 or iron deficiencies. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why might a patient with acute leukemia have swollen, bleeding gums?

options.A: Abnormal white blood cells infiltrate and build up in the gum tissue
options.B: Excessive red blood cells cause high pressure in mouth capillaries
options.C: The patient forgot to brush their teeth for several weeks
options.D: Saliva production completely stops due to bone marrow failure

explanation: In certain leukemias, immature white blood cells crowd into soft tissues like the gums, causing them to swell and bleed easily. Keep up the good reading! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which sign in an enlarged lymph node strongly points toward cancer (malignancy)?

options.A: Soft, tender, and mobile
options.B: Small, rubbery, and painful
options.C: Hard, fixed, and painless
options.D: Warm, pulsating, and soft

explanation: Cancerous lymph nodes are typically firm or hard, stuck tightly in place (fixed), and usually don't hurt when you press them. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the correct way to feel (palpate) lymph nodes during a physical exam?

options.A: Scratching firmly across the skin surface with fingernails
options.B: Pinching the skin tightly between thumb and index finger
options.C: Using the finger pads in gentle circular motions
options.D: Pressing hard with a single thumb until the patient winces

explanation: Always use gentle circular motions with your finger pads. This helps you roll the nodes against the tissue underneath without pushing them away or hurting the patient. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why might you hear a systolic flow murmur in a patient with severe anemia?

options.A: Turbulent blood flow from high cardiac output
options.B: Blood leaking backward through a stiff mitral valve
options.C: Infection of the outer lining of the heart muscle
options.D: A physical hole in the ventricular septum wall

explanation: Because the heart is pumping a larger volume of blood much faster to fight the lack of oxygen, it creates a rushing, turbulent sound that we hear as a flow murmur. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which finding is most commonly auscultated in the lungs of a patient experiencing fluid overload?

options.A: High-pitched whistling wheezes
options.B: Absent breath sounds on the left
options.C: A loud friction rub over the trachea
options.D: Fine crackles at the lung bases

explanation: Fluid backing up into the tiny air sacs of the lungs creates a crackling sound when air pops them open during inhalation. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is the medical term for an abnormally enlarged spleen?

options.A: Hepatomegaly
options.B: Lymphadenopathy
options.C: Cardiomegaly
options.D: Splenomegaly

explanation: Splenomegaly means an enlarged spleen. You'll often see this when the spleen is overworked from filtering out abnormal blood cells. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h6)

question: You feel an organ extending past the left rib margin during a deep abdominal exam. What organ are you most likely feeling?

options.A: Kidney
options.B: Liver
options.C: Pancreas
options.D: Spleen

explanation: The spleen hangs out in the upper left side of the abdomen. If it's enlarged, it extends downward from beneath the left ribs where you can feel it. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h6)

question: Why do patients with multiple myeloma often suffer from severe bone pain?

options.A: Joint cartilage wears down completely from lack of fluid
options.B: Muscles pull too tightly on weak bones during movement
options.C: Nerves wrap tightly around damaged joints in the limbs
options.D: Malignant plasma cells expand inside the bone marrow cavity

explanation: Abnormal plasma cells build up inside the bones, increasing pressure and causing painful damage to the bone structure. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h7)

question: Which nerve-related symptom is commonly linked to a vitamin B12 deficiency?

options.A: Sudden paralysis on one entire side of the body
options.B: Severe sharp pain radiating down the lower back
options.C: Inability to recognize familiar faces or places
options.D: Tingling and numbness in the hands and feet

explanation: Vitamin B12 is super important for nerve health. When you don't have enough, your peripheral nerves get irritated, causing that classic tingling and numbness (paresthesia). [learn more](GNS311_U2_T3#GNS311_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why do blood disorders like sickle cell anaemia often cause deep emotional distress for patients?

options.A: Because of the unpredictable pain crises and lifelong nature of the illness
options.B: Because daily physical therapy is strictly mandatory for everyone
options.C: Because patients get a quick and complete cure in most hospitals
options.D: Because there are never any physical symptoms during early stages

explanation: Living with a chronic condition that flares up unexpectedly takes a heavy mental toll. Understanding this helps you support the whole patient, not just their labs! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h1)

question: As a nurse, why shouldn't you focus only on the physical symptoms of a blood disorder?

options.A: Hospital management policies require psychological notes for discharge
options.B: Physical symptoms are rarely relevant to the patient's actual recovery
options.C: Emotional distress and physical pain deeply affect overall quality of life
options.D: Blood disorders only impact the emotional state of the patient

explanation: Spot on! Holistic nursing means remembering that a patient's mind and body are connected. Healing involves caring for both. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h1)

question: When is the best time to check the psychosocial needs of a patient with a chronic blood disorder?

options.A: Exclusively on the first day of the initial hospital visit
options.B: Whenever the patient requests a change in their medication
options.C: As an ongoing process throughout the course of the illness
options.D: Only during the final stage of palliative care admission

explanation: A patient's worries change as their illness progresses. Checking in regularly lets you catch new stress early! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h2)

question: You want to know how a newly admitted patient is coping emotionally with a sickle cell crisis. What is the best way to ask?

options.A: Wait until the patient brings up mental health issues on their own
options.B: Ask closed yes-or-no questions to speed up your nursing documentation
options.C: Use open-ended questions to invite the patient to share their feelings
options.D: Focus strictly on pain scores and laboratory blood test results

explanation: Open-ended questions like 'How are you holding up today?' give patients the safe space they need to truly open up. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which of these is a healthy, adaptive way for a patient to cope with a chronic illness?

options.A: Isolating oneself completely from friends and family
options.B: Seeking social support and talking about their feelings
options.C: Refusing all prescribed medications out of pure frustration
options.D: Pretending that no physical symptoms exist at all

explanation: Reaching out and talking it out helps patients process stress constructively. We all need a support system! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h3)

question: Why is it risky to ignore signs of depression in a patient managing a blood disorder?

options.A: Depression automatically causes an immediate drop in haemoglobin levels
options.B: Patients with depression are legally barred from receiving blood transfusions
options.C: Sadness always leads to permanent physical paralysis if left unmanaged
options.D: Untreated depression can severely reduce treatment adherence and self-care

explanation: When patients feel hopeless, they might skip clinic visits or meds. Spotting depression early keeps them on track with their healing. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h3)

question: What does the term 'caregiver burden' usually mean in clinical practice?

options.A: The paperwork required by insurance companies for blood products
options.B: The financial cost charged by the hospital for daily inpatient admission
options.C: The physical and emotional strain experienced by family members providing care
options.D: The legal responsibility nurses hold for medication administration errors

explanation: Family caregivers often pour all their energy into the patient and forget themselves, leading to deep fatigue and burnout. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h4)

question: How does having a chronic blood disorder in the family commonly affect household dynamics?

options.A: It permanently removes all forms of conflict between family members
options.B: It ensures that every relative shares equal responsibility for nursing care
options.C: It stops family members from worrying about the patient's future
options.D: It shifts financial duties and alters daily roles within the household

explanation: A long-term illness disrupts normal routines, forcing families to hustle together, adjust budgets, and share new caregiving tasks. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a common financial or social barrier to healthcare access in Nigeria?

options.A: High out-of-pocket expenses for routine medications and blood tests
options.B: Financial strain caused by the loss of daily income during hospital admissions
options.C: Free and unlimited universal healthcare coverage for all citizens
options.D: Long travel distances from rural villages to tertiary teaching hospitals

explanation: If only! Sadly, free universal healthcare isn't the reality yet, meaning out-of-pocket costs remain a huge hurdle for many patients. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the best nursing response when a patient believes their blood disorder is caused entirely by spiritual forces?

options.A: Report the family to hospital security for refusing modern medicine
options.B: Ignore their cultural belief completely and talk only about drugs
options.C: Respect their beliefs while gently providing education on the medical condition
options.D: Scold the patient and family for holding unscientific ideas

explanation: Respect builds trust! When patients feel heard, they are much more willing to listen to your medical guidance. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h5)

question: A patient tells you they are terrified they might die. Which response shows therapeutic communication?

options.A: Leaving the room immediately to let them calm down on their own
options.B: Changing the subject quickly so the patient doesn't start crying
options.C: Validating their feelings and offering a supportive, listening presence
options.D: Telling them not to worry because modern medicine can cure anything

explanation: Just sitting with a frightened patient and saying 'I am here for you' is sometimes the most powerful medicine you can offer. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why is it best for nurses to avoid giving false reassurance like 'everything will be fine'?

options.A: It damages trust when the patient experiences inevitable complications or pain
options.B: It forces the doctor to change the patient's medication prescription
options.C: It is against hospital policy to use comforting words with adults
options.D: It automatically increases the patient's blood pressure and heart rate

explanation: Patients know when things are tough. Being honest and supportive builds a much stronger bond than empty promises. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h6)

question: In the multidisciplinary healthcare team, who typically acts as the central coordinator for day-to-day patient concerns?

options.A: The laboratory scientist
options.B: The pharmacist
options.C: The nurse
options.D: The hospital accountant

explanation: Because you spend the most time at the bedside, you are the bridge connecting the patient, doctors, and other specialists! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h7)

question: A patient with a chronic blood disorder is stressed about overwhelming hospital bills and housing issues. Who should you involve in their care plan?

options.A: An intensive care physician
options.B: A surgical theatre technician
options.C: A hospital physiotherapist
options.D: A medical social worker

explanation: Social workers are absolute lifesavers when it comes to connecting families with financial aid, welfare, and community support. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is the main thing we look at in haematological tests?

options.A: Electrical activity in the heart
options.B: Lung capacity and breathing
options.C: Kidney filtration and urine output
options.D: Blood and blood-making tissues

explanation: Haematology is all about studying blood cells and the tissues, like bone marrow, that make them. You've got this! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why can a blood problem cause symptoms all over the body?

options.A: The lymphatic system traps blood proteins
options.B: Blood flows through every single organ system
options.C: Bone marrow is found in many bones
options.D: Blood cells change shape quickly in the air

explanation: Since blood travels everywhere in the body, when something is off with our blood components, it can show up as tiredness, weakness, or bruising anywhere. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h1)

question: What does a pale inner eyelid or pale nail bed usually point to?

options.A: High blood pressure
options.B: Dehydration
options.C: Anaemia
options.D: An infection

explanation: Paleness in the mucous membranes and nails is a classic sign that the red blood cell count or haemoglobin is low, which we call anaemia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h2)

question: A patient has tiny, pinpoint red spots on their skin called petechiae. What is the nurse most likely to suspect?

options.A: Too much stored iron
options.B: High red blood cell volume
options.C: High white blood cell count
options.D: Platelet problems

explanation: Petechiae are tiny spots of bleeding under the skin that happen when platelets are low or not working right to keep blood vessels sealed. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h2)

question: On a full blood count lab report, what does the abbreviation MCV stand for?

options.A: Minimum capillary vessel
options.B: Measured cellular viscosity
options.C: Mean corpuscular volume
options.D: Maximum clotting velocity

explanation: MCV tells us the average size of the red blood cells. It's super helpful for figuring out what kind of anaemia a patient has! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h3)

question: When is a doctor or lab scientist most likely to order a peripheral blood smear along with a regular full blood count?

options.A: As a quick kidney check before surgery
options.B: To check how much iron the patient eats over time
options.C: When the standard blood count shows unexpected results
options.D: To replace measuring total haemoglobin

explanation: A blood smear lets the lab actually look at the cells under a microscope when the numbers on the regular blood test look a bit strange. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the main difference between a bone marrow aspiration and a bone marrow biopsy?

options.A: Biopsy checks cell maturity, while aspiration checks bone strength
options.B: Biopsy uses arm veins, while aspiration uses the sternum
options.C: Aspiration needs general anaesthesia, but biopsy does not
options.D: Aspiration takes liquid, while a biopsy takes a solid piece of tissue

explanation: Think of aspiration as taking a fluid sample of the marrow, while a biopsy takes a tiny solid cylinder of bone and marrow to check its structure. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is the most important nursing duty right after a patient has a bone marrow test?

options.A: Stop them from drinking any fluids for 12 hours
options.B: Take off the pressure dressing in five minutes
options.C: Get them up to do heavy exercises
options.D: Watch the puncture site closely for bleeding

explanation: Because the needle goes right into the bone, keeping an eye on the site for bleeding or swelling is a top priority to keep your patient safe. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h4)

question: Which lab test is used to monitor a patient taking the blood thinner warfarin?

options.A: Prothrombin Time and INR
options.B: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.C: Activated partial thromboplastin time
options.D: Full blood count with differential

explanation: PT and INR are the go-to tests to make sure a patient on warfarin is getting just the right dose—not too thick, not too thin! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h5)

question: What does a high D-dimer blood test result usually mean?

options.A: Blood clots have recently formed and broken down in the body
options.B: The patient is not eating enough iron
options.C: There are zero platelets left in the blood
options.D: There is a sudden bacterial infection in the blood

explanation: D-dimer is a leftover protein fragment when a clot dissolves. If it's high, it tells us clotting and breakdown have been happening recently. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h5)

question: What technology does flow cytometry use to help diagnose conditions like leukaemia?

options.A: Cell surface markers
options.B: X-ray beams
options.C: Electrical heart signals
options.D: Urine dipsticks

explanation: Flow cytometry uses special tags to spot unique proteins on the outside of abnormal blood cells, helping doctors pinpoint the exact issue. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h6)

question: Why do doctors order genetic tests like FISH or karyotyping for blood cancers?

options.A: To find the patient's blood group for a transfusion
options.B: To find specific chromosome changes and gene mutations
options.C: To measure how much blood was lost in surgery
options.D: To see how fast red blood cells settle in a tube

explanation: Looking at the genetic makeup of the cancer cells helps the medical team figure out the best treatment plan for the patient. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h6)

question: Which imaging scan is commonly used to stage lymphomas by checking for swollen lymph nodes?

options.A: Pulmonary function test
options.B: Computed tomography (CT) scan
options.C: Electroencephalogram (EEG)
options.D: Electrocardiogram (ECG)

explanation: A CT scan gives clear, slice-by-slice pictures that show the size and location of lymph nodes and organs inside the body. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h7)

question: What is a big advantage of a PET scan over a standard CT scan in cancer care?

options.A: It highlights active areas to tell scar tissue apart from live tumor
options.B: It can be done instantly at the bedside without a machine
options.C: It measures the exact amount of haemoglobin in red cells
options.D: It uses no radiation and needs no dye

explanation: PET scans track cellular activity, helping doctors see if a leftover mass is still active cancer or just harmless scar tissue. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h7)

question: What is an immediate nursing action when critical lab results come back from the lab?

options.A: Throw the lab report away if the patient looks fine
options.B: Call the primary doctor with the critical values right away
options.C: Wait until the end of your shift to write them down
options.D: Ask the patient to figure out what their lab results mean

explanation: Critical lab values mean danger! Prompt communication with the medical team keeps your patient safe from harm. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h8)

question: Why is emotional support and clear teaching so important for patients undergoing tests for blood disorders?

options.A: Kind words replace the need for local numbing medicine
options.B: Patients must memorize all lab ranges before going home
options.C: Clear explanations keep the lab machines from breaking down
options.D: The tests often look for serious illnesses like cancer, which causes high worry

explanation: Waiting for results on serious conditions can be terrifying. Your gentle reassurance and clear explanations make a world of difference for a worried patient. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h8)

question: What is the main problem in the body when someone has anaemia?

options.A: Increased thickness of the blood plasma
options.B: Rapid destruction of blood platelets
options.C: Too many white blood cells
options.D: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood

explanation: You've got this! Anaemia simply means the blood doesn't have enough red blood cells or hemoglobin to carry the oxygen your body needs to function well. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why does a person's heart beat faster when they have severe anaemia?

options.A: To warm up body tissues chilled by slow blood flow
options.B: To compensate for lower oxygen delivery by pumping blood faster
options.C: To lower high blood pressure from extra red blood cells
options.D: To help the kidneys filter out waste quickly

explanation: Think of it this way: since each drop of blood carries less oxygen, the heart has to pump much faster to make sure vital organs get what they need! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h1)

question: What is the most common nutritional shortage that causes microcytic anaemia?

options.A: Protein shortage
options.B: Vitamin C lack
options.C: Iron deficiency
options.D: Calcium deficiency

explanation: Great to know for clinicals! Without enough iron, the body cannot build proper hemoglobin, leaving red blood cells looking small and pale. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h2)

question: Lab results show a patient has large (macrocytic) red blood cells. Which vitamin shortage should you check for first?

options.A: Vitamin B12 or folate
options.B: Vitamin D and calcium
options.C: Iron and copper
options.D: Potassium and sodium

explanation: Spot on! Vitamins B12 and folate act like master builders for DNA during red blood cell growth. Without them, the cells grow too large instead of maturing properly. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h2)

question: What is the most common sign you will hear patients complain about when they have anaemia?

options.A: Sudden vision loss
options.B: Fatigue and weakness
options.C: Severe joint swelling
options.D: Uncontrolled tremors

explanation: Makes total sense, right? When tissues are starved of oxygen, patients will constantly feel tired, heavy-limbed, and lacking in energy. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h3)

question: Why do patients with anaemia often have very pale skin and nail beds?

options.A: There is less red hemoglobin pigment in surface blood vessels
options.B: Blood is completely blocked from reaching the skin surface
options.C: The skin makes extra melanin to protect itself
options.D: Poor circulation causes fluid to collect under the skin

explanation: Hemoglobin is what paints our blood red. When levels drop, that healthy pink color fades from places close to the surface, like the palms, gums, and nail beds. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h3)

question: Which standard lab test checks a patient's hemoglobin and hematocrit levels directly?

options.A: Complete blood count
options.B: Coagulation screen
options.C: Basic metabolic profile
options.D: Liver function panel

explanation: The good old Full Blood Count (or Complete Blood Count) is your go-to test for looking at red cells, hemoglobin, and all things blood-related in the ward! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h4)

question: What does a serum ferritin blood test tell the healthcare team?

options.A: Circulating blood sugar
options.B: Active vitamin B12 levels
options.C: Red blood cell lifespan
options.D: Stored iron reserves

explanation: Think of ferritin as the body's iron savings account. A serum ferritin test lets you see how much iron is safely tucked away in storage. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h4)

question: What is the primary goal when treating a patient with anaemia?

options.A: To identify and treat the underlying cause
options.B: To permanently stop all dietary iron intake
options.C: To permanently increase the white blood cell count
options.D: To lower the body temperature to resting levels

explanation: You can't just slap a band-aid on anaemia! Finding out *why* it's happening—whether it's blood loss, heavy periods, or poor nutrition—is key to fixing it. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h5)

question: A patient is taking oral iron pills. What advice should you give them to help their body absorb the iron better?

options.A: Take the supplement with vitamin C or orange juice
options.B: Crush the pills and mix them into a yogurt meal
options.C: Swallow the tablets immediately after drinking a glass of milk
options.D: Take the medication right before going to sleep at night

explanation: Vitamin C is iron's best friend! It creates an acidic environment in the stomach that helps the body absorb oral iron much more effectively. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h5)

question: Why should you schedule planned rest breaks for a hospitalized patient with severe anaemia?

options.A: To lower blood pressure before giving medications
options.B: To give the digestive tract time to process iron pills
options.C: To prevent blood clots from forming in the legs
options.D: To reduce the overall oxygen demand on the body

explanation: Resting lowers the body's workload, which saves precious oxygen for a patient who tires out easily. Pacing is key in nursing care! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h6)

question: What is your most important duty during the first fifteen minutes of a blood transfusion?

options.A: Elevate the head of the bed to a high Fowler position
options.B: Flush the intravenous tubing quickly with dextrose solution
options.C: Stay with the patient and monitor for acute transfusion reactions
options.D: Draw another blood sample from a peripheral vein

explanation: Safety first! Most dangerous transfusion reactions happen right at the beginning, so staying by the bedside to watch your patient is a must. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h6)

question: What serious long-term problem can happen if severe, chronic anaemia is ignored?

options.A: Heart failure
options.B: Bone softening
options.C: Liver cirrhosis
options.D: Kidney stones

explanation: If the heart is forced to pump extra fast for months or years to move oxygen-poor blood, the heart muscle eventually gets exhausted and begins to fail. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h7)

question: A patient calls the clinic panicking because their stool turned dark green after starting iron pills. What should you tell them?

options.A: Advise them to stop taking the iron tablets immediately and rush to the hospital
options.B: Reassure them that this is a harmless and expected side effect
options.C: Tell them to collect a stool sample to check for bleeding
options.D: Tell them to drink less water because it dilutes the drug

explanation: No need to panic! Unabsorbed iron naturally turns the stool dark green or black as it passes through. Giving this quick reassurance eases patient anxiety instantly. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h7)

question: What is the primary abnormal type of haemoglobin found in sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Haemoglobin C
options.B: Haemoglobin F
options.C: Haemoglobin S
options.D: Haemoglobin A

explanation: Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a genetic mutation that produces abnormal haemoglobin S, which distorts red blood cells into a sickle shape when oxygen levels drop. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why do red blood cells turn into a crescent shape in sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Continuous exposure to high fever melts the cell membrane
options.B: White blood cells attack the outer membrane of normal red blood cells
options.C: The bone marrow produces cells with too much iron and too little water
options.D: Haemoglobin S molecules stick together and form stiff rods inside the cell

explanation: You've got this! When haemoglobin S releases its oxygen, the molecules clump together into rigid structures. This pushes the cell membrane into that classic crescent or sickle shape. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h1)

question: In young children with sickle cell anaemia, what is dactylitis?

options.A: Severe infection of the lung tissue
options.B: Painful swelling of the hands and feet
options.C: Sudden yellowing of the eyes and skin
options.D: Abnormal enlargement of the liver

explanation: Dactylitis is often one of the very first signs of sickle cell disease in babies. It happens when sickled cells block blood flow in the tiny bones of the hands and feet, causing painful swelling. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h2)

question: Why do patients with sickle cell anaemia often have chronic jaundice (yellow eyes and skin)?

options.A: The rapid destruction of fragile sickled red blood cells releases excess bilirubin
options.B: The liver fails to produce enough bile salts for normal digestion
options.C: Chronic low-grade kidney failure traps yellow waste products in the skin
options.D: Blocked blood vessels in the pancreas cause a backup of digestive enzymes

explanation: Think of it this way: sickle cells break down much faster than normal round red blood cells. This rapid breakdown releases a lot of bilirubin into the blood faster than the liver can clear it, turning the skin and eyes yellow. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h2)

question: Which laboratory test is used to definitively diagnose sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.B: Coagulation profile test
options.C: Complete blood count
options.D: Haemoglobin electrophoresis

explanation: Haemoglobin electrophoresis is the gold standard test! It separates different types of haemoglobin in a sample so the lab can clearly spot abnormal haemoglobin S. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h3)

question: Why is newborn screening so important for babies with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: It prevents the spleen from ever being damaged by blocked blood vessels
options.B: It stops red blood cells from ever changing into a crescent shape
options.C: It allows early penicillin prophylaxis and vaccination before severe infections occur
options.D: It cures the genetic mutation completely before symptoms start to show

explanation: Early detection saves lives! Finding the condition early lets doctors start daily penicillin and special vaccines right away, protecting the baby from dangerous infections. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h3)

question: Which set of symptoms points strongly to acute chest syndrome in a hospital patient?

options.A: Painful swelling of the hands and feet
options.B: Yellow skin, dark urine, and severe fatigue
options.C: Chest pain, fever, and a new cough
options.D: Headache, dizziness, and sudden blurry vision

explanation: Spotting acute chest syndrome early is a key nursing skill. It acts a lot like pneumonia, showing up with chest pain, fever, and coughing because sickled cells or infections get trapped in the lungs. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h4)

question: A patient with sickle cell anaemia suddenly complains of a severe headache and trouble speaking. What is your priority nursing action?

options.A: Administer a mild oral pain reliever and reassess the patient in one hour
options.B: Perform a prompt neurological assessment and notify the primary provider immediately
options.C: Encourage the patient to drink two large glasses of cold water right away
options.D: Apply a warm compress to the forehead and turn off the overhead room lights

explanation: Trust your nursing instincts! Sudden neurological changes in a sickle cell patient can mean a stroke is happening. This is a medical emergency that needs immediate action. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why should you avoid using cold compresses to treat pain during a sickle cell crisis?

options.A: Refrigerated items increase the risk of skin breakdown over swollen joints
options.B: Cold temperatures cause blood vessels to constrict and promote further sickling
options.C: Low temperatures stop intravenous pain medications from working properly
options.D: Cold packs numb the skin so the patient cannot feel if the pain is improving

explanation: Remember: cold makes blood vessels narrow (vasoconstriction). This slows down blood flow even more, making the sickled cells clump together worse and increasing the patient's pain. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h5)

question: What is the main goal of giving lots of intravenous (IV) fluids during a pain crisis?

options.A: To lower the patient's body temperature and stop low-grade fevers
options.B: To dilute circulating bilirubin and immediately clear skin jaundice
options.C: To stimulate the bone marrow to produce healthy round red blood cells
options.D: To reduce blood viscosity and help clear microvascular blockages

explanation: Fluids are great medicine here! Giving IV fluids thins out the blood (reduces viscosity), helping it flow more easily past those tiny blockages caused by sickled cells. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h5)

question: How does the medication hydroxyurea help treat sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: It increases the production of foetal haemoglobin
options.B: It binds directly to iron stores to prevent liver damage
options.C: It destroys white blood cells to prevent chronic inflammation
options.D: It dilates peripheral blood vessels to lower blood pressure

explanation: Hydroxyurea is a fantastic drug for this condition. It tricks the body into making more foetal haemoglobin, which stops haemoglobin S from clumping together and prevents cells from sickling. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h6)

question: Why must patients on long-term, frequent blood transfusions be closely watched for iron overload?

options.A: Repeated transfusions cause the spleen to stop filtering waste products from plasma
options.B: Donor blood contains high levels of artificial preservatives that damage kidney tissues
options.C: Iron is rapidly absorbed through the intestinal walls during a blood transfusion
options.D: The human body cannot easily excrete excess iron received from donor red blood cells

explanation: Our bodies are great at holding onto iron, but we have no easy way to get rid of extra amounts! Every blood transfusion adds more iron, which can slowly build up and damage vital organs like the heart and liver. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h6)

question: Why do young children with sickle cell anaemia take daily preventive penicillin?

options.A: To thin the blood and stop red blood cells from clumping together
options.B: To stimulate the bone marrow to create more red blood cells
options.C: To lower the body temperature and prevent sudden high fevers
options.D: To protect against severe infections caused by functional asplenia

explanation: Over time, sickle cell damage makes the spleen stop working well (functional asplenia). Because the spleen is vital for fighting certain bacteria, daily penicillin acts as a shield to keep these kids safe from severe infections. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a common trigger for a sickle cell pain crisis?

options.A: Dehydration from drinking too little water
options.B: An underlying viral or bacterial infection
options.C: Exposure to sudden cold weather environments
options.D: Eating a diet high in green leafy vegetables

explanation: Green leafy vegetables are healthy and safe! Infections, cold weather, and not drinking enough water are the real troublemakers that trigger a painful crisis. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h7)

question: Which environmental situation should a patient with sickle cell anaemia avoid to prevent a crisis?

options.A: High humidity during the rainy season
options.B: High-altitude travel with low oxygen levels
options.C: Bright sunlight reflecting off sandy beaches
options.D: Loud noises in crowded public marketplaces

explanation: High altitudes mean less oxygen in the air. For someone with sickle cell, low oxygen can quickly cause red blood cells to sickle, triggering a painful crisis or trouble breathing. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h8)

question: How does teaching lifestyle habits help a patient with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: It cures the genetic condition entirely through proper daily nutrition and rest
options.B: It guarantees that they will never experience chronic fatigue or joint pain again
options.C: It teaches them how to safely perform their own blood transfusions at home
options.D: It helps them avoid common triggers like dehydration and extreme cold to prevent crises

explanation: Knowledge is power! When patients know what sets off a crisis—like staying hydrated or dressing warmly—they can take charge of their daily health and stay out of the hospital. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h8)

question: What is the main feature of polycythaemia?

options.A: A dangerous drop in blood platelets
options.B: A sudden drop in white blood cells
options.C: An abnormal increase in red blood cells
options.D: Too much fluid loss from blood vessels

explanation: You've got this! Polycythaemia simply means an overproduction of red blood cells in the body. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h1)

question: Why does having too many red blood cells make work harder for the heart?

options.A: It destroys the heart muscle walls
options.B: It causes severe body dehydration
options.C: It makes blood thick and slows down flow
options.D: It stops oxygen from being made

explanation: Think of it like porridge! Extra red cells make the blood thick and syrupy, so the heart has to pump much harder. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h1)

question: What is another common name for primary polycythaemia?

options.A: Polycythaemia vera
options.B: Secondary erythrocytosis
options.C: Iron deficiency anemia
options.D: Aplastic anemia

explanation: Primary polycythaemia is also called polycythaemia vera. It happens right inside the bone marrow stem cells! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h2)

question: What usually triggers the body to develop secondary polycythaemia?

options.A: An autoimmune attack on bone marrow
options.B: An inherited defect in the platelets
options.C: Sudden heavy blood loss from injury
options.D: Chronic low oxygen levels in tissues

explanation: Spot on! When body tissues are short on oxygen over time, the body panics and pumps out more red blood cells to help. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h2)

question: Which genetic change is most often linked to primary polycythaemia vera?

options.A: JAK2 mutation
options.B: BRCA1 mutation
options.C: CFTR mutation
options.D: Factor V Leiden

explanation: A mutation in the JAK2 gene is the classic signature of primary polycythaemia vera. It tells the bone marrow to keep dividing cells non-stop. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h3)

question: A patient with long-term chronic bronchitis is most at risk for which blood issue?

options.A: Acute blood loss anemia
options.B: Primary polycythaemia from a tumor
options.C: Secondary polycythaemia from low oxygen
options.D: Hemolytic anemia from cell damage

explanation: Great connection! Bronchitis makes breathing hard, leading to low oxygen, which then triggers secondary polycythaemia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h3)

question: What does the term 'plethora' mean in a patient with polycythaemia?

options.A: Severe swelling in the lower legs
options.B: A ruddy, reddish skin complexion
options.C: Yellow discoloration of the eyes
options.D: A sudden drop in blood pressure

explanation: Plethora just describes that classic red or flushed face look because there are so many blood cells packed near the skin surface. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why do some polycythaemia patients feel very itchy after a warm bath?

options.A: Infection of skin pores by bacteria
options.B: Release of histamine from blood cells
options.C: Allergic reaction to tap water
options.D: Rapid drying of the skin from heat

explanation: Warm water opens up skin vessels, releasing histamine from blood cells and causing that annoying, intense itch! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h4)

question: How do blood erythropoietin levels help tell primary and secondary polycythaemia apart?

options.A: Primary has high levels, secondary has zero
options.B: Hormone levels stay normal in both conditions
options.C: Primary has low levels, secondary has high levels
options.D: Both types always show very low hormone levels

explanation: In primary, the bone marrow acts on its own, so the body stops making erythropoietin. In secondary, the body pumps out extra erythropoietin because it's begging for oxygen! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h5)

question: Which test directly confirms a diagnosis of polycythaemia vera?

options.A: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.B: JAK2 gene mutation assay
options.C: Coagulation profile test
options.D: Serum iron and ferritin panel

explanation: Running a JAK2 gene test is the go-to way to confirm primary polycythaemia vera at the cellular level. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h5)

question: What is the main goal of therapeutic phlebotomy in polycythaemia?

options.A: To increase blood pressure
options.B: To remove excess white blood cells
options.C: To provide iron for the liver
options.D: To reduce red blood cell mass and hematocrit

explanation: Phlebotomy is just safely removing some blood to lower the packed cell volume (hematocrit) and thin things out! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h6)

question: As a nurse, what is a key care step for a patient being treated for polycythaemia?

options.A: Giving high-dose iron with meals
options.B: Restricting all physical movement to bed rest
options.C: Applying warm compresses to the legs
options.D: Encouraging plenty of fluids to stop sluggish blood

explanation: Fluid is key! Drinking enough water keeps the thick blood moving smoothly and prevents dangerous clots. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h6)

question: Why might a patient with high blood cell counts paradoxically face bleeding risks?

options.A: The body stops making fibrinogen completely
options.B: The excess platelets do not function right
options.C: Phlebotomy removes all clotting proteins
options.D: High blood pressure bursts skin capillaries

explanation: Even though platelet numbers look high, they are often faulty and don't do their clotting job properly, leading to bleeding worries. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a typical long-term complication of untreated polycythaemia vera?

options.A: Iron deficiency anemia from suppressed bone marrow
options.B: Progression into acute leukemia
options.C: Transformation into myelofibrosis
options.D: Arterial and venous blood clots

explanation: Polycythaemia is all about having *too many* red blood cells, not iron deficiency anemia. Clots and bone marrow changes are the real long-term risks to watch out for. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h7)

question: What is the main job of normal lymphocytes in our body?

options.A: Fighting off infections and foreign invaders
options.B: Producing red blood cells in the bone marrow
options.C: Clotting blood to prevent bleeding
options.D: Carrying oxygen to body tissues

explanation: Think of lymphocytes as part of your body's security team! They are white blood cells that protect you against bacteria, viruses, and other germs. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h1)

question: What happens inside the body to cause lymphoma?

options.A: Lymph vessels become blocked and burst
options.B: Abnormal lymphocytes multiply out of control and form tumors
options.C: The spleen stops filtering old cells
options.D: Bone marrow permanently stops making white cells

explanation: Lymphoma happens when those protective white blood cells (lymphocytes) go wild, dividing without stopping and building up in the lymph nodes. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h1)

question: Which special cell type must be present to diagnose Hodgkin Lymphoma?

options.A: Epithelial cells
options.B: Reed-Sternberg cells
options.C: Plasma cells
options.D: Kupffer cells

explanation: Spotting giant, unusual Reed-Sternberg cells under a microscope is the classic giveaway that tells doctors it's Hodgkin Lymphoma! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h2)

question: How does Hodgkin lymphoma typically spread compared to non-Hodgkin types?

options.A: It only affects organs in the lower belly
options.B: It never spreads outside the bone marrow
options.C: It spreads in an orderly, predictable pattern
options.D: It jumps randomly to distant body parts immediately

explanation: Hodgkin lymphoma is like a polite traveler—it usually moves step-by-step to neighboring lymph nodes, making its path pretty predictable. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h2)

question: Which childhood lymphoma is very common in malaria-endemic regions like Nigeria?

options.A: Multiple myeloma
options.B: Chronic myeloid leukemia
options.C: Burkitt lymphoma
options.D: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia

explanation: Burkitt lymphoma is well-known in tropical Africa. It's often linked with the Epstein-Barr virus and chronic exposure to malaria. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h3)

question: Why does a weak immune system raise a person's risk for lymphoma?

options.A: Red blood cells lose their ability to carry iron
options.B: The bone marrow completely stops making platelets
options.C: Lymph vessels expand and trap toxins
options.D: The body fails to stop abnormal cell growth and viral triggers

explanation: When your immune system's security guard is sleeping (weakened), viruses and mutated cells can slip past and multiply unchecked. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h3)

question: What are unexplained fevers, night sweats, and weight loss in lymphoma called?

options.A: B symptoms
options.B: Metabolic syndrome
options.C: Constitutional markers
options.D: A symptoms

explanation: In clinical practice, we group these classic warning signs—fever, drenching night sweats, and weight loss—together as 'B symptoms'. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h4)

question: A patient is admitted with suspected lymphoma. What is the most common early physical sign a nurse expects to find?

options.A: Severe skin rashes over the tummy
options.B: Painless, enlarged lymph nodes in the neck
options.C: Complete paralysis of both legs
options.D: Bleeding gums and sudden nosebleeds

explanation: Keep an eye out for this: the earliest and most common sign is a lump in the neck that swells up without causing any pain. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the gold standard test to confirm a diagnosis of lymphoma?

options.A: Complete blood count
options.B: Excisional lymph node biopsy
options.C: Routine skin scraping
options.D: Fine-needle aspiration cytology

explanation: To be 100% sure, pathologists need to look at a whole lymph node under the microscope. Taking out the node (excisional biopsy) is the best way to do this. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h5)

question: According to the Ann Arbor staging system, what defines Stage III lymphoma?

options.A: Spread to distant organs like the liver
options.B: Lymph node involvement on both sides of the diaphragm
options.C: Disease found only in the tummy area
options.D: Involvement of just a single lymph node

explanation: Think of the diaphragm as a dividing line. Stage III means enlarged nodes are hanging out both above AND below that breathing muscle. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h5)

question: How do targeted drugs like rituximab help fight lymphoma cells?

options.A: By blocking all blood vessels feeding the tumor
options.B: By attaching to cell markers and flagging them for immune destruction
options.C: By replacing damaged DNA strands inside the cell
options.D: By telling the liver to make extra clotting factors

explanation: Targeted therapy acts like a smart missile. It sticks to a specific tag on the cancer cell so your immune system can spot and destroy it easily. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h6)

question: Why do doctors use a combination of different chemotherapy drugs instead of just one?

options.A: To completely eliminate all side effects
options.B: To target only upper-body lymph nodes
options.C: To finish the entire treatment in a single afternoon
options.D: To attack cancer cells through different angles and prevent drug resistance

explanation: Using a combo team of drugs hits the cancer from multiple directions, making it much harder for the sneaky cancer cells to find a way to resist. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h6)

question: A patient on chemotherapy has a dangerously low neutrophil count. What is your most critical nursing action?

options.A: Massaging swollen lymph nodes firmly every few hours
options.B: Enforcing strict hand hygiene and restricting sick visitors
options.C: Encouraging fresh, unwashed garden salads
options.D: Administering live polio vaccines

explanation: Low neutrophils mean low infection-fighting power! Hand hygiene and keeping germs away are absolute lifesavers here. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h7)

question: What is the main goal of scheduling rest periods for a patient with cancer-related fatigue?

options.A: Stimulating the appetite center in the brain
options.B: Preventing blood clots in the legs
options.C: Helping the patient conserve energy while staying gently active
options.D: Shrinking peripheral lymph node masses

explanation: It's all about balance! Alternating rest with light activity helps patients manage their energy without losing all their muscle strength. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h7)

question: Which complication involves facial swelling, neck vein bulging, and trouble breathing due to a blocked chest vein?

options.A: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation
options.B: Superior Vena Cava Obstruction
options.C: Tumor Lysis Syndrome
options.D: Spinal Cord Compression

explanation: When a chest tumor presses on the big superior vena cava vein, blood gets backed up—leading to that classic puffy face and neck swelling. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h8)

question: What causes the chemical imbalances known as Tumor Lysis Syndrome?

options.A: Eating too many potassium-rich foods during chemo
options.B: Severe dehydration from vomiting
options.C: Sudden failure of the thyroid gland
options.D: Massive, rapid destruction of cancer cells releasing their contents into the blood

explanation: When chemo works *too* fast, millions of cancer cells burst open at once, spilling their insides (like potassium and uric acid) straight into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h8)

question: When is the best time to bring in palliative care for a patient diagnosed with lymphoma?

options.A: Only during the final 24 hours of life
options.B: Alongside regular curative treatment right from the start
options.C: Only when the patient asks for hospice
options.D: After all chemotherapy options have failed

explanation: Palliative care isn't just for end-of-life; it's about comfort and symptom relief, and it works best when started early alongside cancer treatment! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h9)

question: A patient finishing treatment is terrified the cancer will return. How should the nurse respond?

options.A: Promise them that cancer never, ever comes back
options.B: Tell them to stop thinking about their health history
options.C: Acknowledge their fear and discuss healthy coping and follow-up plans
options.D: Refer them for emergency surgery immediately

explanation: Fear of a comeback is completely normal for survivors. Validating their feelings and showing them the clear follow-up plan brings real peace of mind. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h9)

question: What is the main job of sensory receptors in our special senses?

options.A: Pump blood through the sensory organs
options.B: Convert environmental stimuli into electrical signals
options.C: Store memories of past sensory experiences
options.D: Produce hormones to regulate body temperature

explanation: Think of sensory receptors as tiny translators! They take physical things from the world around us—like light or sound—and change them into electrical signals that our nervous system can easily read and understand. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h1)

question: How are special senses different from general senses?

options.A: Special senses are housed in complex, distinct organs in the head
options.B: Special senses only function while a person is sleeping
options.C: General senses do not use electrical impulses to communicate
options.D: General senses are controlled entirely by the spinal cord

explanation: Unlike touch receptors that are spread all over your body, special senses like sight, taste, and hearing have their own specialized, dedicated homes in the head, like the eyes and tongue! [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which part of the retina helps us see sharp, colorful images in bright light?

options.A: Cones
options.B: Cornea
options.C: Lens
options.D: Rods

explanation: You can remember 'Cones for Color'! Cones are the hardworking cells in our eyes that give us clear details and vibrant colors when the lights are bright. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h2)

question: Why are our eyes so dependent on rod cells when we are trying to see in the dark?

options.A: Rods block out distracting light rays in dark rooms
options.B: Rods are located only in the front part of the cornea
options.C: Rods are extremely sensitive to low levels of light
options.D: Rods produce the pigments needed to see bright colors at night

explanation: Rods don't do color very well, but they are night-vision champions! They only need a tiny glimmer of light to help us spot shapes and shadows in the dark. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h2)

question: What is the main job of the tiny bones (ossicles) in the middle ear?

options.A: Equalize air pressure behind the eardrum
options.B: Amplify and transmit sound vibrations to the inner ear
options.C: Produce earwax to protect the ear canal
options.D: Translate electrical signals into spoken words

explanation: These three little bones act like a sound system amplifier. When sound hits your eardrum, they boost the vibration and pass it smoothly into the inner ear fluid. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h3)

question: A patient complains of constant dizziness and trouble keeping their balance. Which part of the ear is likely involved?

options.A: External ear canal
options.B: Auditory ossicles
options.C: Tympanic membrane
options.D: Semicircular canals

explanation: The semicircular canals in your inner ear are your body's built-in spirit level. They track your head movements and help keep you balanced. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT one of the five basic tastes?

options.A: Umami
options.B: Salty
options.C: Bitter
options.D: Spicy
