explanation: You got it! Staging lets the team know how far the cancer has spread, which helps them choose the best treatment plan and understand what lies ahead. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which of these is a key responsibility for a nurse working in public health cancer advocacy?

options.A: Organizing community awareness and teaching early detection methods
options.B: Diagnosing cancer stages without the need for pathology reports
options.C: Performing independent surgical removal of malignant tumors
options.D: Manufacturing chemotherapy medications in hospital pharmacies

explanation: Brilliant! Nurses play a leading role in public health by educating communities, spreading awareness, and encouraging early screening. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h7)

question: A community nurse notices women in a village avoiding breast screening due to cultural fears. What is the best way to handle this?

options.A: Report the village residents to local government authorities for non-compliance
options.B: Insist that screening is mandatory under all circumstances
options.C: Ignore the cultural beliefs and hand out clinical pamphlets silently
options.D: Provide culturally sensitive health education and address community fears openly

explanation: Spot on! Building trust through gentle, respectful conversations and addressing fears openly is always the best nursing approach for community health. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h7)

question: What is the very first step in how cancer starts in the body?

options.A: Chronic dehydration of body tissues
options.B: Excessive intake of dietary proteins
options.C: Rapid spread of bacteria in the blood
options.D: Genetic mutation in a single cell

explanation: Cancer kicks off when a change happens in a cell's genes, making it grow and divide without stopping. You've got this! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why is the nurse's role so important when a patient is first told they might have cancer?

options.A: To determine the final pathological tumor grade
options.B: To perform surgical removal of the tumor mass
options.C: To prescribe and administer initial chemotherapy doses
options.D: To reduce anxiety and guide patients through complex tests

explanation: Finding out about cancer is super scary. Nurses step in as guides and educators to help patients understand tests and calm their fears. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which special scan uses a tiny, safe radioactive substance to check for active changes in body tissues?

options.A: Basic fluoroscopy
options.B: Ultrasound
options.C: PET scan
options.D: Standard X-ray

explanation: A PET scan uses a special tracer to light up how tissues and organs are working on a cellular level. Pretty neat technology! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h2)

question: A healthy 50-year-old woman asks why she needs a routine mammogram when she feels fine. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Routine screening is legally required for all women over the age of forty in this country.
options.B: Screening tests catch cancer early before symptoms develop, which makes treatment more successful.
options.C: These tests are designed to prevent normal cells from ever mutating into cancerous growths.
options.D: Mammograms are only performed after a physician feels a distinct lump during a physical exam.

explanation: Screening is all about catching things early before they turn into bigger problems. Early detection makes treatment much easier! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h2)

question: What does tumor 'staging' mainly tell the healthcare team?

options.A: The exact microscopic appearance and shape of the cells
options.B: The size of the tumor and how far it has spread
options.C: The speed at which the patient's hair falls out
options.D: The specific type of chemotherapy needed for cure

explanation: Staging helps doctors figure out how big the tumor is and if it has traveled to other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h3)

question: How do high-grade cancer cells usually act compared to low-grade cancer cells?

options.A: High-grade cells never metastasize to lymph nodes.
options.B: High-grade cells are easier to destroy with basic antibiotics.
options.C: High-grade cells look identical to healthy tissue under a lens.
options.D: High-grade cells grow and spread much more rapidly.

explanation: High-grade cells are fast-growing and more aggressive, meaning doctors need to act quickly. You're doing great learning this! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why is a biopsy a must-have test when checking for cancer?

options.A: It replaces the need for laboratory blood testing entirely.
options.B: It lowers systemic blood pressure during diagnostic scans.
options.C: It completely cures the patient by removing all toxins.
options.D: It provides definitive microscopic proof of malignancy.

explanation: Looking at actual cells under a microscope is the only way to be 100% sure whether cancer cells are present. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the nurse's main job right after a tissue sample (biopsy) is taken?

options.A: Place the tissue sample in a household refrigerator until the morning shift
options.B: Examine the cells under the ward microscope to give an early report
options.C: Wash the specimen with sterile water to remove any residual blood
options.D: Ensure correct labeling and prompt placement in the proper preservative solution

explanation: Good lab results start with proper handling! Labeling it right away and putting it in the right preservative keeps the sample safe for testing. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the most important nursing check right after a patient has a liver biopsy?

options.A: Remove all intravenous access lines right away
options.B: Monitor vital signs and check the puncture site for bleeding
options.C: Feed the patient a large high-fiber meal immediately
options.D: Encourage the patient to walk briskly around the hospital ward

explanation: Since the liver has a huge blood supply, watching closely for bleeding and checking vital signs is top priority after this procedure. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h5)

question: A patient scheduled for a procedure with mild sedation asks for a glass of water an hour beforehand. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Explain that fasting guidelines must be followed to prevent aspiration during sedation.
options.B: Ignore the question because fluid intake does not affect anesthesia safety.
options.C: Tell the patient to drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated before the test.
options.D: Allow the patient to drink a small cup of water since it is just a liquid.

explanation: Fasting (NPO) keeps the stomach empty so the patient doesn't accidentally choke or inhale stomach contents while sedated. Safety first! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h5)

question: How should a nurse respond when a patient is extremely scared while waiting for biopsy results?

options.A: Tell them not to worry because most lumps turn out to be harmless
options.B: Remind them that other patients have much worse conditions
options.C: Change the subject immediately to cheer them up
options.D: Acknowledge their feelings and listen attentively to their concerns

explanation: Just being there, listening, and validating their worries can be a huge comfort to a terrified patient. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h6)

question: What is a very normal emotional reaction for patients waiting to find out if they have cancer?

options.A: Uncontrolled physical hunger
options.B: Extreme happiness and relief
options.C: Intense anxiety and shock
options.D: Complete emotional numbness

explanation: Waiting for big health news is terrifying. Shock and heavy anxiety are very common reactions that nurses need to be ready to support. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which medical expert spends their day looking at tissue samples under a microscope to diagnose cancer?

options.A: Dietitian
options.B: Pathologist
options.C: Surgeon
options.D: Radiologist

explanation: Pathologists are the lab detectives who study cells and tissues to give us a clear diagnosis. Teamwork makes the dream work! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h7)

question: Why do healthcare workers use a team approach (doctors, nurses, pharmacists, etc.) in cancer care?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any nursing involvement in patient education.
options.B: It reduces hospital costs by avoiding diagnostic imaging tests.
options.C: It combines various specialties to ensure accurate diagnosis and comprehensive treatment planning.
options.D: It allows a single doctor to make all clinical decisions without consulting others.

explanation: Cancer care is complex! Working together ensures that every single physical, emotional, and medical need of the patient is met. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h7)

question: During which phase of the cell cycle does a cell make a copy of its DNA?

options.A: First gap phase
options.B: Mitotic phase
options.C: Resting phase
options.D: Synthesis phase

explanation: You got this! The S phase (synthesis phase) is specifically when the cell replicates its genetic material before dividing. Think 'S' for 'Synthesis' or 'Copying'! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h1)

question: What is the main job of checkpoints in the normal cell cycle?

options.A: To stop division if DNA damage is found
options.B: To speed up tissue growth
options.C: To provide energy for the cell to split
options.D: To turn active cells into resting cells

explanation: Great try! Cell checkpoints act like security guards—they inspect the cell and halt the cycle if anything looks damaged, keeping the body safe. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h1)

question: When one mature cell type changes into another mature cell type due to ongoing irritation, what is it called?

options.A: Anaplasia
options.B: Hyperplasia
options.C: Metaplasia
options.D: Apoptosis

explanation: Spot on! Metaplasia is like a cellular makeover; cells switch to a tougher type to better handle chronic stress, such as smoke irritation in the airways. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h2)

question: A lab report describes tissue with disordered growth and cells of varying shapes and sizes. Which term describes this?

options.A: Metaplasia
options.B: Dysplasia
options.C: Hyperplasia
options.D: Atrophy

explanation: Well done! Dysplasia means disordered growth where cells lose their normal shape and organization—often an early warning sign that nurses watch closely. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h2)

question: What do we call the process where cancer cells break away and spread through the blood or lymph to other parts of the body?

options.A: Mitosis
options.B: Metastasis
options.C: Metaplasia
options.D: Apoptosis

explanation: You're doing great! Metastasis happens when malignant cells travel via blood or lymph to set up secondary growths in distant organs. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h3)

question: Which of these is a typical feature of a benign (non-cancerous) tumor?

options.A: Surrounded by a fibrous capsule
options.B: Infiltrates surrounding normal tissues
options.C: Rapid and uncontrolled cellular division
options.D: Ability to form secondary tumors

explanation: Correct! Benign tumors usually stay put inside a neat fibrous capsule, meaning they don't invade nearby tissues or spread around. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h3)

question: What are the two big features that define all stem cells?

options.A: Programmed death and shrinkage
options.B: Rapid mutation and anaplasia
options.C: Self-renewal and potency
options.D: Encapsulation and metastasis

explanation: Spot on! Stem cells are amazing because they can both make copies of themselves (self-renewal) and turn into specialized cells (potency). [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why is cellular differentiation so important for the human body?

options.A: It ensures that all cells in the body remain identical
options.B: It stops normal cells from resting
options.C: It allows basic cells to mature into specific functional cells
options.D: It keeps the immune system calm

explanation: Brilliant! Differentiation is how a simple stem cell becomes a specialized muscle, nerve, or blood cell to do specific jobs in the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h4)

question: What is the main underlying cause of uncontrolled cell growth in cancer?

options.A: Accumulated mutations in cellular DNA
options.B: Permanent resting state in the cells
options.C: A total lack of cellular respiration
options.D: Eating too many vitamins

explanation: You've got it! Cancer starts when genetic errors build up over time, breaking the normal rules that tell cells when to stop growing. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h5)

question: Why do advanced tumors often become resistant to medical treatments like chemotherapy?

options.A: The body's immune system destroys the medication before it reaches the tumor
options.B: Chemotherapy drugs turn normal cells into malignant cancer cells
options.C: Genetic diversity creates varied cell populations with different drug resistance traits
options.D: Tumor cells develop a protective bone shell that blocks all medications

explanation: As mutations accumulate, cancer cells become diverse; while some cells die from treatment, resistant clones survive and multiply. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is the normal, healthy job of proto-oncogenes in our bodies?

options.A: Triggering cell suicide immediately
options.B: Encapsulating benign tumors
options.C: Promoting normal cell growth and division
options.D: Repairing broken DNA strands

explanation: Spot on! Proto-oncogenes are normal, helpful genes that tell cells when it's time to grow and repair tissues. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h6)

question: What happens when a tumor suppressor gene experiences a loss-of-function mutation?

options.A: The cell immediately transforms into a benign fibrous cyst
options.B: The cell loses its molecular brakes and divides uncontrollably
options.C: The cell creates an outer capsule to prevent metastasis
options.D: Normal cellular division stops permanently in the G0 phase

explanation: Tumor suppressor genes normally slow down cell growth; losing them removes these protective brakes, allowing rapid tumor growth. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the main role of apoptosis in the body?

options.A: Removing damaged or unneeded cells in a neat, orderly way
options.B: Causing sudden inflammation after an injury
options.C: Turning normal tissue into tumors
options.D: Encouraging rapid stem cell division

explanation: Correct! Apoptosis is the body's clean-up process—it gently removes old or damaged cells without causing messy inflammation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h7)

question: How do cancer cells frequently manipulate apoptosis to survive and multiply?

options.A: They trigger excessive external death receptor signals
options.B: They replace damaged mitochondria with healthy ones
options.C: They mutate regulatory genes to evade programmed cell death
options.D: They speed up the intrinsic pathway to destroy healthy tissue

explanation: Cancer cells often survive by disabling the normal suicide signals that would normally force a damaged cell to die. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h7)

question: Why do traditional chemotherapy drugs commonly cause side effects like hair loss and mucosal sores?

options.A: They cause the patient's immune system to attack hair follicles
options.B: They attack all rapidly dividing cells, both cancerous and normal
options.C: They block the formation of protective fibrous tumor capsules
options.D: They stimulate normal cells to enter permanent resting phases

explanation: Traditional chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells, which inadvertently damages healthy tissues with high turnover like hair follicles and gut linings. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h8)

question: A patient on chemotherapy has a very low white blood cell count. What is the top nursing priority?

options.A: Stopping the process of metastasis
options.B: Giving medication to help hair grow back
options.C: Preparing the patient for emergency surgery
options.D: Monitoring closely for signs of infection

explanation: Brilliant nursing judgment! Low white blood cells (neutropenia) mean the immune system is weak, so watching for and preventing infection is your #1 priority. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h8)

question: What is the literal meaning of the medical term neoplasm?

options.A: Inflamed tissue
options.B: Normal healing
options.C: New growth
options.D: Cell death

explanation: The term neoplasm comes from Greek roots meaning new formation or growth, which describes the abnormal tissue mass formed by runaway cell division. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why do neoplastic cells form a tumor instead of behaving normally?

options.A: They expand rapidly because they are fighting off local infections
options.B: They grow larger to replace dead tissue in the organ
options.C: They absorb too much water from surrounding blood vessels
options.D: They multiply uncontrollably due to failed growth regulation

explanation: You've got this! Normally, our body tells cells when to rest and when to divide. In a tumor, those control signals fail, and the cells just keep multiplying without stopping. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which feature is typical of a benign tumor?

options.A: It destroys neighboring healthy organs
options.B: It is enclosed by a fibrous capsule
options.C: It looks completely different from normal cells
options.D: It spreads quickly through the bloodstream

explanation: Benign growths typically form a distinct capsule that separates them from surrounding tissue, making them easier to excise. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h2)

question: Even though a benign tumor is non-cancerous, why can it still be dangerous to a patient?

options.A: It always releases toxic poisons into the bloodstream
options.B: It can press on vital structures inside confined spaces
options.C: It frequently turns into widespread blood cancer
options.D: It destroys the immune system completely

explanation: Think about a crowded room! Even if things are peaceful, if a tumor grows inside a tight space like the skull, it can press on vital organs and cause serious trouble. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is the term for cancer cells spreading to distant parts of the body?

options.A: Metastasis
options.B: Hyperplasia
options.C: Angiogenesis
options.D: Differentiation

explanation: Metastasis occurs when malignant cells break free, enter circulation or lymph channels, and establish secondary tumor sites far from the original growth. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h3)

question: Why do fast-growing malignant tumors encourage angiogenesis (the growth of new blood vessels)?

options.A: It causes the tumor cells to mature and look normal
options.B: It stops the tumor from spreading to other organs
options.C: It helps cancer cells hide from white blood cells
options.D: It creates new blood vessels to supply oxygen and nutrients

explanation: Clever! Tumors need food and oxygen to keep growing rapidly. By triggering angiogenesis, they force the body to build a dedicated supply line straight to them. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h3)

question: What do we call a cancer that starts in the epithelial tissue lining body surfaces?

options.A: Sarcoma
options.B: Myeloma
options.C: Leukemia
options.D: Carcinoma

explanation: You're doing great! Carcinomas are the most common type of cancer because they start in the skin and the cells lining our internal organs and body surfaces. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h4)

question: A patient is diagnosed with a tumor growing in the smooth muscle of the thigh. Which classification applies best?

options.A: Sarcoma
options.B: Carcinoma
options.C: Lymphoma
options.D: Leukemia

explanation: Connective and supportive tissues like muscle, bone, and fat give rise to sarcomas rather than carcinomas. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h4)

question: What does the 'T' stand for in the TNM cancer staging system?

options.A: Tumor size and extent
options.B: Tissue toxicity
options.C: Total body weight
options.D: Treatment schedule

explanation: In the TNM system, T evaluates the size and direct extent of the primary tumor, N assesses lymph node involvement, and M checks for distant metastasis. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h5)

question: How is cancer grading different from cancer staging?

options.A: Grading counts white blood cells, while staging counts red blood cells
options.B: Grading is only used for benign tumors, while staging is for malignant ones
options.C: Grading looks at cellular appearance under a microscope, while staging looks at how far the cancer has spread
options.D: Grading measures organ failure, while staging measures treatment success

explanation: Think of it this way: Grading checks how 'wild' or abnormal the cells look under a microscope, while staging looks at the map of the body to see how far the cancer has traveled. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a common side effect of chemotherapy that nurses watch out for?

options.A: Permanent tissue encapsulation
options.B: Severe fatigue
options.C: Increased infection risk
options.D: Bone marrow suppression

explanation: You've got this! Encapsulation is a trait of benign, harmless-looking growths, not a side effect of chemo. Chemo hits fast-dividing cells, which often leads to fatigue and low blood counts. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h6)

question: A patient on chemotherapy has a very low white blood cell count. What should be your top nursing priority?

options.A: Administering high doses of oral iron supplements
options.B: Encouraging heavy physical exercise to combat fatigue
options.C: Preparing the patient for immediate surgical tumor removal
options.D: Protecting the patient from potential sources of infection

explanation: Brilliant nursing logic! White blood cells are our body's soldiers. When their count drops (neutropenia), our main job is to guard the patient fiercely against any germs and infections. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h6)

question: What is the main thing that happens in neoplasia?

options.A: Uncontrolled and uncoordinated cellular proliferation
options.B: Rapid healing of acute tissue damage
options.C: Temporary swelling caused by local infection
options.D: Normal replacement of dead skin cells

explanation: Think of neoplasia as new growth that just won't quit! The cells keep multiplying without listening to the body's normal stop signals. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why do cancer cells keep growing even after the original tissue injury is gone?

options.A: They receive constant growth signals from nearby nerves
options.B: Scar tissue forces them to keep dividing rapidly
options.C: The body actively pumps extra blood into the tumor
options.D: Their internal regulatory machinery is permanently damaged

explanation: You got this! Inside these cells, the internal control buttons are broken, so they keep multiplying on their own without needing an outside trigger. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h1)

question: Which of these is a classic feature of a benign tumor?

options.A: It grows very fast and invades nearby muscle
options.B: It has poorly differentiated, weird-looking cells
options.C: It easily spreads through the lymphatic system
options.D: It stays localized inside a fibrous capsule

explanation: Benign is friendly! These tumors stay neatly wrapped up in their own little capsule and don't try to invade the surrounding tissues. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h2)

question: What makes a malignant tumor much more dangerous than a benign one?

options.A: Their tendency to cause severe local pain within days of starting
options.B: The fact that they always grow much larger than benign lumps
options.C: The complete absence of blood vessels inside their tissue mass
options.D: The ability to invade nearby structures and spread to distant organs

explanation: Malignant cells are troublemakers because they don't stay put. They love to break away and travel to other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h2)

question: What happens when a normal proto-oncogene gets mutated?

options.A: It turns into an oncogene that drives nonstop cell division
options.B: It immediately forces the cell to undergo programmed death
options.C: It repairs all surrounding damaged DNA strands instantly
options.D: It stops all cellular activity and puts the cell to sleep

explanation: Proto-oncogenes are like the gas pedal for cell growth. When mutated, they become oncogenes that push the pedal all the way down! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h3)

question: What is the normal job of a tumor suppressor gene in a healthy cell?

options.A: act as a brake on cell division and fix DNA errors
options.B: stimulate rapid tissue repair after a physical injury
options.C: transport waste products away from dividing cells
options.D: supply extra blood and oxygen to growing tissues

explanation: Think of tumor suppressor genes as the safety brakes. They slow down cell division and patch up any DNA mistakes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h3)

question: What is the very first thing that happens during the initiation phase of cancer development?

options.A: The immune system completely destroys the mutated cell
options.B: New blood vessels sprout to feed the growing tumor mass
options.C: Abnormal cells spread through blood to distant organs
options.D: Permanent damage or mutation happens to the cell DNA

explanation: Initiation is the starting spark—it's that first permanent hit or change to the cell's DNA caused by a carcinogen. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h4)

question: During which phase of cancer development do cells gain aggressive traits and learn to spread?

options.A: Progression
options.B: Initiation
options.C: Promotion
options.D: Encapsulation

explanation: Progression is the final, full-speed-ahead phase where the cells become truly malignant and start invading. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h4)

question: What chemical signal do growing tumors release to tell new blood vessels to grow?

options.A: Insulin-like growth hormone
options.B: Vascular endothelial growth factor
options.C: Red blood cell stimulating protein
options.D: Platelet aggregation factor

explanation: VEGF is the chemical helper tumors use to build their own private highway system of blood vessels (angiogenesis). [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h5)

question: Why do growing malignant tumors desperately need angiogenesis?

options.A: It supplies necessary oxygen and nutrients while removing metabolic waste
options.B: It provides a hard outer shell that keeps the tumor tightly enclosed
options.C: It protects the tumor cells from being destroyed by radiation therapy
options.D: It prevents white blood cells from attacking the cancerous mass

explanation: Just like us, tumors need food and oxygen to keep growing, plus a way to take out the trash! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h5)

question: What special tools do cancer cells use to break through surrounding tissue barriers?

options.A: Matrix metalloproteinases
options.B: Gastric digestive pepsins
options.C: Liver clotting factors
options.D: Insulin receptor enzymes

explanation: MMPs act like little scissors or chemical drills, helping cancer cells chew through the matrix and invade surrounding tissue. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h6)

question: A patient has colon cancer, and a scan shows the cancer has now traveled to the liver. What is this secondary growth called?

options.A: Metastasis
options.B: Hyperplasia
options.C: Encapsulation
options.D: Angiogenesis

explanation: When cancer cells pack their bags and travel from their original home to a brand new organ, we call it metastasis. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h6)

question: What is the term for the severe muscle wasting and extreme weight loss seen in many advanced cancer patients?

options.A: Metaplasia
options.B: Polycythemia
options.C: Cachexia
options.D: Hypertrophy

explanation: Cancer cachexia is a tough syndrome where the body rapidly wastes away its muscle and fat, despite eating. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h7)

question: What causes paraneoplastic syndromes in cancer patients?

options.A: The cancer spreads directly into the spinal cord and blocks nerve signals
options.B: The patient develops a severe secondary bacterial infection
options.C: Chemotherapy drugs destroy the patient's bone marrow completely
options.D: The tumor releases hormones or proteins that affect distant body systems

explanation: Even though they are far away from the tumor, other organs act up because the tumor secretes confusing hormones and proteins into the blood. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h7)

question: When cancer treatment cannot cure the disease, but aims to stop tumor growth and extend life, what is this main goal called?

options.A: Palliation
options.B: Cure
options.C: Prevention
options.D: Control

explanation: You've got this! When complete cure isn't possible, 'control' is the goal—stopping the cancer from spreading further to help the patient live a longer, fuller life. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why might a cancer care plan shift from trying to cure the disease to focusing purely on comfort and palliation?

options.A: Standard surgical options are suddenly much safer than outpatient chemotherapy.
options.B: The patient's insurance policy has expired and can no longer cover active medications.
options.C: The nursing staff prefers managing comfort care over administering toxic drugs.
options.D: The disease has progressed beyond the point where a cure or control is realistically achievable.

explanation: Spot on! When the disease advances past where treatment can stop it, the healthcare team shifts gears to palliation—focusing entirely on comfort, symptom relief, and quality of life. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h1)

question: What kind of surgery involves removing a healthy organ because a patient has a high genetic risk of getting cancer there later?

options.A: Curative surgery
options.B: Prophylactic surgery
options.C: Diagnostic surgery
options.D: Palliative surgery

explanation: Great thinking! Prophylactic means preventative. Doctors perform this to remove healthy tissue before cancer ever gets a chance to start. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h2)

question: A patient has surgery to remove a bowel tumor just to relieve an active intestinal blockage. What type of surgery is this?

options.A: Diagnostic
options.B: Curative
options.C: Prophylactic
options.D: Palliative

explanation: Well done! Even though it's surgery, it's classified as palliative because its main job is to ease distressing symptoms (like a blockage) rather than cure the cancer itself. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h2)

question: How does external radiation therapy mainly work to destroy cancer cells?

options.A: By chemically dissolving the outer cell wall
options.B: By starving the tumor of blood supply
options.C: By boosting the patient's native immune system
options.D: By damaging the internal DNA of the cells

explanation: You're doing great! Radiation targets the heart of the cell—its DNA—breaking it down so the cancer cells can no longer multiply. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h3)

question: Why do nurses constantly remind patients receiving radiation therapy not to wash off their skin treatment marks?

options.A: To prevent the patient from developing a severe skin allergy to the ink
options.B: To keep the hospital records accurate for billing and insurance purposes
options.C: To allow the radiation oncologists to track how fast the outer tumor is shrinking
options.D: To ensure precise daily alignment of the radiation beam to the exact tumor site

explanation: Spot on! Those little marks are like a bullseye. They make sure the radiation machine hits the exact tumor spot safely every single time. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h3)

question: What nursing term describes when a harsh chemotherapy drug accidentally leaks out of the vein into the surrounding tissue?

options.A: Anaphylaxis
options.B: Extravasation
options.C: Phlebitis
options.D: Infiltration

explanation: You've got this! Extravasation happens when a vesicant drug escapes into surrounding tissues, which can cause serious local tissue damage. Always protect your IV sites! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why do patients on standard chemotherapy often experience hair loss and mouth sores?

options.A: The chemical makeup of the drugs directly dries out the outer layers of human skin.
options.B: The radiation energy absorbed by the bloodstream weakens oral and scalp tissues.
options.C: Patients naturally stop eating enough fresh fruits and vegetables due to nausea.
options.D: The medications attack all rapidly dividing cells, including healthy normal cells like hair follicles and mucosal linings.

explanation: Exactly! Chemotherapy targets fast-growing cells. Sadly, it can't tell the difference between cancer cells and our healthy fast-growing cells, like hair and gut linings. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h4)

question: What is the main way targeted cancer therapy drugs fight the disease?

options.A: They physically trap circulating tumor cells inside the liver.
options.B: They emit local ionizing radiation directly inside the blood vessels.
options.C: They replace the patient's damaged bone marrow with healthy donor cells.
options.D: They block specific molecules and growth pathways unique to cancer cells.

explanation: Brilliant! Unlike regular chemo, targeted therapy acts like a smart missile, zeroing in on specific chemical signals that tumors use to grow. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is a major risk for patients taking immune checkpoint inhibitors (immunotherapy)?

options.A: The medication causes immediate permanent sterility in both male and female patients.
options.B: The boosted immune system may attack normal, healthy organs, causing widespread inflammation.
options.C: The drug destroys bone marrow production completely, requiring lifelong platelet transfusions.
options.D: The patient will instantly lose all hair follicles within forty-eight hours of the first dose.

explanation: You got it! Reviving the immune system is great for fighting cancer, but sometimes the revved-up immune cells accidentally attack healthy organs like the lungs or gut. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which emergency shows up as facial swelling, upper body congestion, and swollen neck veins because a major blood vessel is blocked?

options.A: Febrile neutropenia
options.B: Spinal cord compression
options.C: Tumor lysis syndrome
options.D: Superior vena cava syndrome

explanation: Awesome work! When a tumor presses on the superior vena cava, blood backs up from the upper body, causing that classic facial and neck swelling. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h6)

question: A cancer patient on chemo has a fever of 38.5°C and a very low neutrophil count. What is your immediate priority action?

options.A: Wait for routine morning blood cultures to return before calling the physician.
options.B: Administer prescribed broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately.
options.C: Encourage the patient to drink large volumes of cold citrus juices.
options.D: Apply an ice blanket to bring down the patient's core body temperature.

explanation: Safety first! Febrile neutropenia is a life-threatening emergency. Quick IV antibiotics are vital to stop rapid-fire sepsis in its tracks. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h6)

question: When assessing a patient's pain, what is always considered the most reliable indicator?

options.A: The physical size and location of the tumor
options.B: The observable heart rate and blood pressure
options.C: The patient's personal self-report
options.D: The nurse's professional clinical judgment

explanation: Spot on, future nurse! Pain is subjective. If the patient says it hurts, it hurts—their word is always our gold standard for assessment. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h7)

question: Why do nurses give anti-nausea (antiemetic) medications *before* chemotherapy starts, instead of waiting for nausea to begin?

options.A: Chemotherapy drugs lose their chemical potency if antiemetics are not circulating beforehand.
options.B: Patients will refuse their chemotherapy infusions entirely if they feel even a slight hint of nausea.
options.C: Proactive antiemetic dosing ensures the patient remains fast asleep throughout the entire procedure.
options.D: It is much easier to prevent nausea from developing than to stop it once it has already started.

explanation: You're totally right! Prevention is key here. Stopping nausea signals before they trigger makes treatment way more tolerable for the patient. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h7)

question: At what point in their journey can a cancer patient start receiving palliative care?

options.A: When the patient's life expectancy drops below two weeks
options.B: Once the patient is admitted to a dedicated hospice facility
options.C: At the time of diagnosis, alongside active curative treatments
options.D: Only after all forms of chemotherapy and radiation have failed

explanation: Brilliant! Palliative care isn't just for end-of-life; it can—and should—start right from diagnosis to help manage symptoms while active treatment happens. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h8)

question: How does general palliative care differ from standard hospice care?

options.A: Palliative care is only provided in outpatient clinics, while hospice care is strictly for hospital inpatients.
options.B: Palliative care can be given alongside curative treatments, whereas hospice care begins when curative treatment has stopped.
options.C: Palliative care is managed entirely by physicians, whereas hospice care is run strictly by volunteers.
options.D: Palliative care focuses exclusively on spiritual counseling, while hospice care manages physical pain.

explanation: You nailed it! Think of hospice as a specific type of palliative care reserved for the final phase of life, while general palliative care can start on day one. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the main difference between localized cancer treatments and systemic treatments?

options.A: Localized treatments are always surgical while systemic treatments are always oral
options.B: Systemic therapies only affect the specific organ where the tumor originally started
options.C: Systemic therapies travel through the bloodstream to reach cells throughout the body
options.D: Localized treatments cure cancer completely while systemic treatments only relieve pain

explanation: You've got this! Systemic treatments enter the bloodstream, which lets them reach cancer cells that might have traveled away from the main tumor site. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why is it important for nurses to know if a cancer treatment is meant to cure the disease or provide comfort (palliative)?

options.A: It dictates whether the patient is allowed to receive any form of nutrition by mouth
options.B: Palliative regimens mean the patient no longer requires physical assessments or lab work
options.C: Curative regimens require nurses to administer medications without checking vital signs
options.D: It helps guide realistic patient expectations, monitoring priorities, and supportive care planning

explanation: Great nursing insight! Knowing the main goal of treatment helps you plan the best supportive care and keep patient expectations clear and hopeful. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why does chemotherapy often cause hair loss and upset stomach lining?

options.A: Chemotherapy drugs specifically seek out and destroy healthy tissues
options.B: These areas of the body have a much higher temperature than others
options.C: Patients fail to eat enough nutritious food during their hospital stay
options.D: These normal tissues consist of cells that divide very rapidly

explanation: Spot on! Chemo targets fast-dividing cells. Because our hair and gut lining naturally grow fast, they get affected too along with the cancer cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h2)

question: A nurse is about to give a vesicant chemo drug through a hand vein. What is the most crucial check before starting?

options.A: Instructing the patient to tightly flex their arm muscles throughout the entire infusion
options.B: Warming the intravenous fluid bag to body temperature to prevent vein spasms
options.C: Verifying brisk blood return to confirm the catheter is properly placed inside the vein
options.D: Diluting the concentrated medication with sterile water instead of normal saline

explanation: Wonderful safety check! Vesicants can severely damage surrounding skin if they leak, so always check for blood return first to make sure you are safely in the vein. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h2)

question: How do targeted therapy drugs differ from traditional chemotherapy?

options.A: They work exclusively by boosting the overall white blood cell count in the bloodstream
options.B: They can only be taken as topical creams applied directly to skin lesions
options.C: They completely rebuild the patient's bone marrow within forty-eight hours of administration
options.D: They focus on specific molecular targets involved in tumor growth rather than attacking all dividing cells

explanation: You're doing great! Targeted therapies act like smart missiles, zeroing in on specific cancer proteins instead of harming all fast-growing cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a typical side effect of immune checkpoint inhibitors?

options.A: Inflammation of the colon leading to severe diarrhea
options.B: Immune-mediated pneumonitis causing breathing difficulties
options.C: Permanent structural damage to the heart muscle valves
options.D: Dermatitis and itchy rashes across the skin surface

explanation: You got this right! These drugs ramp up the immune system, causing inflammatory side effects like rashes or gut issues, but heart valve destruction isn't a hallmark of this class. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h3)

question: What is the main goal of hormone therapy in certain cancers?

options.A: To permanently increase the patient's natural testosterone and estrogen levels
options.B: To block or lower hormone levels that stimulate the growth of hormone-sensitive tumors
options.C: To completely replace failing endocrine glands throughout the entire body
options.D: To stimulate rapid production of red blood cells to prevent severe anemia

explanation: Exactly! Some cancers love hormones to grow. Hormone therapy cuts off that fuel supply to slow them down. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h4)

question: A patient on hormone therapy for prostate cancer reports hot flashes and fatigue. How should you understand these symptoms?

options.A: Evidence of severe bone marrow suppression caused by the treatment
options.B: Early indicators of metastatic cancer spreading to the brain
options.C: Signs of an acute allergic reaction to the oral medication
options.D: Expected side effects resulting from artificially lowered hormone levels

explanation: Spot on! Lowering hormones mimics natural changes like menopause or andropause, which often brings tiredness and hot flashes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h4)

question: How does external radiation therapy primarily destroy cancer cells?

options.A: By using high-energy rays to damage cellular DNA and stop cell division
options.B: By lowering the patient's core body temperature to induce cellular death
options.C: By surgically removing the affected organ through a small skin incision
options.D: By flooding the circulatory system with cytotoxic chemical compounds

explanation: Well done! Radiation uses targeted high-energy beams to break the DNA inside cancer cells so they can't multiply anymore. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h5)

question: A patient receiving neck radiation asks if they can use their favorite scented lotion on the area. What is the best reply?

options.A: Recommend using only approved, gentle, fragrance-free products to avoid further skin irritation
options.B: Suggest stopping all skin hygiene practices until the entire course of treatment finishes
options.C: Advise scrubbing the skin firmly with a washcloth before applying any cream or lotion
options.D: Encourage applying the scented lotion generously right before each radiation session

explanation: You're thinking like a caring nurse! Radiation makes skin very sensitive, so stick to mild, fragrance-free lotions approved by the care team. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h5)

question: Why is a low white blood cell count (neutropenia) a medical emergency for patients on chemotherapy?

options.A: It prevents the kidneys from filtering normal metabolic waste products
options.B: It leads to severe joint stiffness and sudden hair loss across the scalp
options.C: The body loses its primary defense against invading bacteria and pathogens
options.D: It causes immediate, uncontrollable bleeding from small skin cuts

explanation: Spot on! Neutrophils are our infection-fighting soldiers. When they drop, even minor germs can quickly cause serious infections. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h6)

question: A patient undergoing chemotherapy has a platelet count of 45,000/mcL. Which instruction is best?

options.A: Increase intake of green leafy vegetables to boost iron and clotting factors
options.B: Take high-dose aspirin daily to help thin the blood and improve circulation
options.C: Perform vigorous deep-tissue stretching exercises twice a day to prevent stiffness
options.D: Use an electric shaver instead of a traditional razor for daily grooming

explanation: Brilliant! Low platelets mean a higher risk of bleeding, so switching from sharp razors to electric shavers helps keep the patient safe from cuts. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h6)

question: What is the main cause of Tumor Lysis Syndrome when cancer treatment begins?

options.A: Rapid destruction of large numbers of cancer cells releasing contents into the blood
options.B: Bacterial invasion of the bloodstream due to low white blood cell counts
options.C: Severe dehydration caused by prolonged nausea and vomiting after chemotherapy
options.D: A sudden allergic reaction to the intravenous fluids administered in the clinic

explanation: You've got this! When chemo works *too* fast, cells burst open all at once, flooding the blood with waste products that stress the kidneys. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h7)

question: A lung cancer patient reports sudden back pain, weak legs, and trouble passing urine. What emergency should you suspect?

options.A: Tumor lysis syndrome
options.B: Spinal cord compression
options.C: Superior vena cava syndrome
options.D: Febrile neutropenia

explanation: Excellent clinical catch! Back pain plus weakness and bladder issues is a classic red flag for a tumor pressing right on the spinal cord. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h7)

question: When can palliative care start for a patient with advanced cancer?

options.A: At any point during the illness, alongside active curative treatments
options.B: Only when the patient is completely free of all physical pain
options.C: Exclusively during the final forty-eight hours of life in a hospice unit
options.D: Only after all forms of chemotherapy and radiation have failed

explanation: Wonderful to know! Palliative care isn't just for end-of-life; it can start right from diagnosis to help manage symptoms and boost quality of life. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h8)

question: A patient with advanced cancer starts strong opioid pain medication. What preventive care must you include?

options.A: Restricting fluid intake to prevent fluid overload from the oral medications
options.B: Encouraging a low-fiber diet to reduce gastrointestinal activity during treatment
options.C: Checking blood pressure every fifteen minutes to monitor for sudden hypertension
options.D: Administering prescribed stool softeners and laxatives to prevent opioid-induced constipation

explanation: Spot on! Opioids slow down the bowels significantly. Always team them up with a laxative to keep the patient comfortable and safe from constipation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h8)

question: What is the primary focus of critical care nursing?

options.A: Long-term management of stable chronic illnesses at home
options.B: Outpatient screening for common infectious diseases
options.C: Care of patients with unstable, life-threatening conditions
options.D: Routine post-surgical rehabilitation and physical therapy

explanation: Critical care nursing is specifically dedicated to patients whose conditions are unstable and require intensive monitoring. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why did Florence Nightingale place the most severely injured soldiers closest to the nurse's station?

options.A: To make it easier for doctors to perform sudden surgeries
options.B: To keep them away from noisy convalescing soldiers
options.C: To comply with strict military hierarchy rules
options.D: To allow for closer and more frequent observation

explanation: Placing the sickest patients near the nurses allowed staff to detect rapid changes in condition early. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h1)

question: What major global health crisis drove the rapid development of early mechanical ventilation?

options.A: The polio epidemics of the mid-20th century
options.B: The 1918 influenza pandemic across Europe
options.C: Major outbreaks of cholera in crowded cities
options.D: The rapid rise of severe traumatic road accidents

explanation: The polio epidemics caused widespread respiratory paralysis, forcing hospitals to find mechanical ways to help patients breathe. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h2)

question: How did an iron lung primarily help a patient with respiratory paralysis breathe?

options.A: It used negative pressure to expand the chest wall
options.B: It compressed the abdomen to force air out of the lungs
options.C: It electrically stimulated the diaphragm to contract
options.D: It pumped high-pressure oxygen directly into the trachea

explanation: Iron lungs lowered air pressure inside the tank, causing the patient's chest to expand and air to rush into the lungs naturally. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is a defining characteristic of a modern intensive care unit?

options.A: Low staffing levels because patients are mostly stable
options.B: High nurse-to-patient ratios and specialized life support equipment
options.C: Large open wards with minimal monitoring equipment
options.D: Focus primarily on long-term physical therapy and recovery

explanation: ICUs require specialized equipment and close nursing watch due to the extreme instability of the patients admitted there. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h3)

question: What was the main operational breakthrough that led to the creation of the first formal ICU?

options.A: Centralizing critically ill patients and specialized breathing support in one location
options.B: Discovering broad-spectrum antibiotics to cure bacterial infections
options.C: Developing advanced surgical techniques for open-heart operations
options.D: Inventing the first computerized electronic health record system

explanation: Grouping unstable patients together allowed specialized staff to use newly invented ventilation techniques more efficiently. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h3)

question: What primary problem led to the invention of the Coronary Care Unit (CCU)?

options.A: High rates of severe bleeding during routine blood pressure checks
options.B: Sudden, unrecognized lethal heart rhythms causing unexpected cardiac arrests
options.C: A massive shortage of beds for patients suffering from severe pneumonia
options.D: The frequent occurrence of surgical wound infections after heart operations

explanation: CCUs were created to continuously monitor heart patients so dangerous rhythms could be treated immediately before the heart stopped. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h4)

question: How did the role of the nurse change with the introduction of coronary care units?

options.A: Nurses were trained to independently spot dangerous rhythms and start emergency defibrillation
options.B: Nurses handed over all emergency response duties entirely to specialized physicians
options.C: Nurses focused solely on administering oral medications prescribed at shift change
options.D: Nurses were restricted from touching cardiac monitors without direct written doctor orders

explanation: Because cardiac arrest happens instantly, CCU nurses had to be trained to act immediately without waiting for a physician. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h4)

question: What prompted the creation of formal critical care nursing organizations and certification standards?

options.A: The complete elimination of physicians from intensive care units
options.B: A government mandate to reduce the total number of working hospital nurses
options.C: The increasing complexity of patient technology requiring advanced specialized skills
options.D: A sudden drop in the number of students applying to nursing school

explanation: General training could not keep pace with advanced monitors and life support, leading to the creation of specialized critical care nursing standards. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which skill became essential for nurses as critical care established itself as a distinct specialty?

options.A: Managing hospital financial budgets and payroll for nursing units
options.B: Performing major abdominal surgeries independently in an emergency
options.C: Interpreting complex hemodynamic parameters and monitor waveforms
options.D: Conducting long-term outpatient psychiatric counseling sessions

explanation: Specialized nurses learned to read intricate data from monitors to catch subtle signs of patient deterioration early. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which device is commonly managed by modern critical care nurses to support kidney function?

options.A: Automated external pacemaker for heart block
options.B: Negative-pressure iron lung for breathing
options.C: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) machine
options.D: Intra-aortic balloon pump for cardiac support

explanation: CRRT is a specialized form of dialysis used in the ICU for critically ill patients with acute kidney injury. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is a major focus of modern critical care nursing alongside managing advanced technology?

options.A: Discharging patients within twenty-four hours of admission
options.B: Holistic care, managing pain, and preventing ICU delirium
options.C: Limiting family involvement to reduce room contamination
options.D: Focusing entirely on machine maintenance and calibration

explanation: While machines keep patients alive, modern nurses focus heavily on human comfort, psychological well-being, and family support. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is a primary focus for advancing critical care nursing in resource-limited settings like Nigeria?

options.A: Shifting all intensive care services entirely to outpatient clinics
options.B: Replacing all bedside nurses with automated robotic systems
options.C: Eliminating the need for continuous patient vital sign monitoring
options.D: Expanding specialized training and improving access to life support equipment

explanation: Improving education and basic equipment access is vital for strengthening critical care delivery in developing healthcare settings. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h7)

question: How do tele-ICU networks help improve critical care in remote regional hospitals?

options.A: By automatically discharging stable patients without staff help
options.B: By lowering the total cost of hospital room construction
options.C: By replacing physical bedside nurses with video cameras
options.D: By allowing experts to consult on complex cases remotely

explanation: Tele-ICU technology connects regional staff with distant specialists to guide care for unstable patients in real time. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h7)

question: What is the main job of a mechanical ventilator when a patient cannot breathe well on their own?

options.A: To deliver oxygen and remove carbon dioxide
options.B: To keep the patient completely sedated
options.C: To permanently replace natural breathing
options.D: To cure the underlying lung disease

explanation: Think of the ventilator as a helpful partner. It steps in to help with gas exchange—bringing in fresh oxygen and blowing off waste carbon dioxide—until the lungs are strong enough to take over. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h1)

question: Why would a patient with a severe head injury and a dropping Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score be put on a ventilator?

options.A: Airway protection
options.B: Chronic lung disease
options.C: Metabolic alkalosis
options.D: Primary heart failure

explanation: When a patient's level of consciousness drops, they lose the reflex to keep their airway safe. A ventilator tube protects them from choking or swallowing saliva into their lungs. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h1)

question: In ventilator settings, what does the term PEEP stand for?

options.A: Positive end-expiratory pressure
options.B: Primary external air pressure
options.C: Peak elastic expiration pressure
options.D: Pulmonary evaluation and expansion protocol

explanation: PEEP leaves a tiny bit of pressure in the lungs right at the end of a breath. This stops the tiny air sacs from collapsing like deflated balloons! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h2)

question: Which ventilator mode gives a full breath whenever the patient tries to inhale, while also making sure they get a minimum number of breaths per minute?

options.A: Continuous positive airway pressure
options.B: Assist-Control
options.C: Controlled ventilation
options.D: Pressure support alone

explanation: Assist-Control is like a supportive teammate. It senses when the patient wants to breathe and finishes the job for them, but it also has a backup timer just in case. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h2)

question: After putting in an endotracheal tube, what is the quickest and most reliable bedside check to confirm it is in the right place?

options.A: Measuring the blood pressure
options.B: Checking chest expansion visually
options.C: End-tidal carbon dioxide detection
options.D: Listening to the stomach sounds

explanation: Carbon dioxide only comes out of the lungs! Finding CO2 right after the tube goes in proves it is sitting safely in the trachea and not accidentally down the esophagus. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h3)

question: A newly intubated patient is on a ventilator. You notice the left side of the chest is barely moving and you cannot hear breath sounds there. What likely happened?

options.A: The ventilator settings have too much positive end-expiratory pressure
options.B: The tube has slipped into the right mainstem bronchus
options.C: The oxygen source has become disconnected from the machine
options.D: The patient is developing a severe tension pneumothorax

explanation: The right breathing pipe (bronchus) is a straight shot down, so tubes often slide too far in and end up ventilating only the right lung, leaving the left side quiet. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h3)

question: Why can mechanical ventilation sometimes cause a patient's blood pressure to drop?

options.A: The ventilator directly causes vasodilation of peripheral arteries
options.B: Increased chest pressure reduces blood return to the heart
options.C: Sedative medications increase the heart rate too much
options.D: High oxygen levels make blood vessels constrict sharply

explanation: Pumping positive air pressure into the chest creates a tight squeeze around the heart's main blood vessels, making it a bit harder for blood to flow back to the heart temporarily. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h4)

question: What is the recommended angle for lifting the head of the bed for a patient on a mechanical ventilator?

options.A: 30 to 45 degrees
options.B: 0 to 15 degrees
options.C: 60 to 75 degrees
options.D: 90 degrees sitting upright

explanation: Keeping the bed raised between 30 and 45 degrees uses gravity to help stop spit or stomach juices from sliding down into the lungs. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h4)

question: What is the safest maximum time allowed for a single pass of suctioning an endotracheal tube?

options.A: 60 seconds
options.B: 30 to 45 seconds
options.C: 2 to 3 seconds
options.D: 10 to 15 seconds

explanation: When you suction, you are also sucking out the patient's air. Keep it brief (10–15 seconds) so they do not run out of oxygen or get a spike in heart rhythm. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h5)

question: When is the right time to suction a patient who is on a ventilator?

options.A: Every hour on the hour strictly
options.B: Only when clinical signs indicate retained secretions
options.C: Immediately before every physician visit
options.D: Whenever the patient asks for it

explanation: Suctioning is rough on the airways and steals a bit of air. Always assess the patient first and only suction when you actually hear or see signs that they need it! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h5)

question: Which nursing care task is superstar at preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia?

options.A: Keeping the patient completely flat in bed
options.B: Administering high doses of intravenous steroids
options.C: Performing regular chlorhexidine oral care
options.D: Changing the ventilator tubing every shift

explanation: Keeping the mouth clean with chlorhexidine stops bad bacteria from throwing a party in the mouth and sliding down into the vulnerable lungs. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h6)

question: What directly causes barotrauma in a patient on a ventilator?

options.A: Lack of early physical therapy and leg movement
options.B: Inadequate hand hygiene by the nursing staff
options.C: Bacterial infection growing in the endotracheal tube
options.D: High airway pressure or excessive lung volume

explanation: Too much pressure or blowing the lungs up like an over-inflated balloon can pop delicate air sacs, causing air to leak where it shouldn't. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h6)

question: What is the main point of doing a Spontaneous Breathing Trial (SBT)?

options.A: To measure the exact size of the patient's lung capacity
options.B: To clean out thick secretions from the lower airways
options.C: To give the mechanical ventilator a chance to rest and cool down
options.D: To test if the patient can breathe without full ventilator support

explanation: An SBT dials back the machine's help to see if the patient's own breathing muscles are ready to take over the job. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h7)

question: During a breathing trial, your patient starts sweating heavily, using their neck muscles to breathe, and their heart rate shoots from 85 to 130 beats per minute. What should you do?

options.A: Stop the trial and resume previous ventilator support settings
options.B: Encourage the patient to keep trying because anxiety is normal
options.C: Administer a strong sedative medication to calm the patient down
options.D: Remove the endotracheal tube immediately to finish extubation

explanation: Whoops, they are struggling! These are red flags that the breathing trial is failing. Put the ventilator settings right back where they were and let the machine help them rest. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h7)

question: Why should you still talk and explain procedures to a sedated patient on a ventilator?

options.A: It satisfies the legal requirement for written informed consent
options.B: It helps the mechanical ventilator synchronize with the patient's heart
options.C: Unconscious or sedated patients may still perceive and process sound
options.D: Hospital regulations require talking to every patient on a machine

explanation: Hearing is often the last sense to go. Explaining what you are doing is a kind, human act that helps soothe fear and confusion. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h8)

question: What is the best way to help an awake, intubated patient communicate with you?

options.A: Using communication boards or writing tablets
options.B: Asking the patient to whisper loudly around the tube
options.C: Relying entirely on family members to translate lip movements
options.D: Temporarily deflating the cuff on the tube so they can talk

explanation: Because the breathing tube sits right through the vocal cords, speaking is impossible. Simple writing pads or picture boards are a nurse's best friend here! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h8)

question: What is the main job of resuscitative equipment in the ward?

options.A: To provide routine daily patient hygiene care
options.B: To monitor long-term chronic wound healing
options.C: To manage sudden cardiac or respiratory arrest
options.D: To deliver oral medications during meals

explanation: You've got this! Resuscitative tools are kept ready specifically for emergencies when a patient stops breathing or their heart stops. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h1)

question: Why do nurses need to know emergency devices very well before a crisis happens?

options.A: To prevent equipment theft in the ward
options.B: To ensure fast and effective action during high-stress moments
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of hospital supplies
options.D: To avoid having to document patient care tasks

explanation: Spot on! In an emergency, knowing your tools right away helps you act fast and save precious time. You are doing great! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of a bag-valve-mask (BVM) resuscitator?

options.A: To measure blood oxygen saturation
options.B: To deliver positive pressure ventilation
options.C: To visualize the vocal cords clearly
options.D: To suction thick oral secretions

explanation: Great job! You squeeze the BVM manually to push air into the lungs of a patient who cannot breathe on their own. Simple and lifesaving! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h2)

question: A patient vomits heavily during a cardiac arrest. What should the nurse grab right away?

options.A: The suction catheter and canister
options.B: The laryngoscope handle
options.C: The bag-valve-mask resuscitator
options.D: The endotracheal tube stylet

explanation: Well thought out! We must clear vomit immediately using suction so the airway is open and safe for breathing support. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h2)

question: Which device delivers a shock to stop dangerous, irregular heart rhythms?

options.A: An infusion pump
options.B: A suction machine
options.C: A cardiac monitor
options.D: A defibrillator

explanation: Exactly! The defibrillator sends a quick electrical current to reset a chaotic heart back into a steady rhythm. You're mastering this! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h3)

question: Why is setting up an IV line so crucial during a resuscitation?

options.A: To secure the endotracheal tube in place
options.B: To measure the exact volume of carbon dioxide exhaled
options.C: To monitor the patient's core body temperature
options.D: To deliver emergency medications and fluids directly into the bloodstream

explanation: Spot on! An IV line acts like a fast highway to pump life-saving drugs straight into circulation when every second counts. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h3)

question: How often should emergency crash carts and equipment usually be checked?

options.A: Once every month
options.B: Only after a code blue occurs
options.C: At the start of every shift
options.D: During annual hospital accreditation

explanation: Correct! Checking the crash cart every shift ensures everything is present, unexpired, and working before an emergency strikes. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h4)

question: What should you do immediately if you find an expired drug in the crash cart during a check?

options.A: Report and replace it right away
options.B: Leave it until the end of the week
options.C: Use it on the next stable patient
options.D: Hide it in the bottom drawer

explanation: You got it! Expired drugs can fail when you need them most, so swapping them out instantly keeps our patients safe. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h4)

question: What is the best first step if an electrical piece of emergency gear fails to turn on?

options.A: Throw the device out the window
options.B: Abandon resuscitation efforts entirely
options.C: Check the power source and cable connections
options.D: Wait for a biomedical engineer to arrive

explanation: Brilliant! Often, it's just a loose plug or unseated battery that you can fix in seconds. Always check the basics first! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a good safety practice for emergency equipment?

options.A: Conducting regular staff simulation drills
options.B: Ignoring minor device malfunctions
options.C: Documenting equipment maintenance logs
options.D: Debriefing team performance after code events

explanation: Spot on! Never brush off small faults—minor issues can turn into big failures during a real emergency. Keep up the great work! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T11#GNS321_U2_T11_h5)

question: Which body regulates the professional conduct and practice of nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: National Association of Nigerian Nurses and Midwives
options.B: Nigerian Medical Association
options.C: Federal Ministry of Health
options.D: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria

explanation: Spot on! The NMCN is the main statutory body that oversees nursing education and practice standards in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why is it important for nurses to understand healthcare laws?

options.A: To avoid personal liability and protect patient rights in clinical settings
options.B: To replace hospital lawyers during lawsuits
options.C: To prescribe medications independently when doctors are absent
options.D: To bypass getting consent from family members in emergencies

explanation: You got it! Knowing your legal boundaries helps you deliver safe care while keeping your license and patients protected. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h1)

question: What is the term for a nurse's legal obligation to answer for their professional actions?

options.A: Professional accountability
options.B: Informed consent
options.C: Beneficence
options.D: Vicarious liability

explanation: Exactly! Accountability means owning up to both the good and bad outcomes of the care you provide. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h2)

question: A doctor writes a medication dose that looks obviously incorrect for your patient. What should you do?

options.A: Ask a junior colleague to give the drug so blame is shared
options.B: Administer the medication quickly so care isn't delayed
options.C: Ignore the order completely and document nothing
options.D: Clarify the order with the prescriber before giving the medication

explanation: Brilliant! Patient safety comes first. Always pause to clarify any unsafe or confusing orders before you administer anything. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which legal concept allows nurses and doctors to treat an unconscious emergency patient without explicit consent?

options.A: Res ipsa loquitur
options.B: Emergency privilege
options.C: Vicarious liability
options.D: Professional indemnity

explanation: Correct! Emergency privilege assumes a patient would want life-saving care when they are unable to speak for themselves. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h3)

question: Which of these is required for a patient's informed consent to be legally valid?

options.A: A complete guarantee of a successful medical outcome
options.B: Direct verbal instruction from the lead hospital consultant
options.C: Written approval witnessed by a hospital lawyer
options.D: Voluntary agreement without force or pressure

explanation: Spot on! True consent must be given freely by the patient without any form of manipulation or coercion. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of an advanced healthcare directive?

options.A: To permit nurses to alter medical prescriptions independently
options.B: To guarantee financial compensation for hospital admission
options.C: To guide medical treatment choices before a patient loses the ability to decide
options.D: To protect the hospital from paying taxes on equipment

explanation: You nailed it! Advanced directives let people state their medical wishes ahead of time just in case they can't speak later. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h4)

question: Why can carrying out a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order sometimes be challenging in the ward?

options.A: Nurses have final authority to override any DNR request
options.B: Balancing legal directives, family views, and the duty to save lives is complex
options.C: Advanced directives are automatically the same in every culture globally
options.D: Doctors are legally forbidden from writing DNR orders

explanation: Exactly. Emotions, family expectations, and ethics often clash when dealing with end-of-life decisions, making communication very vital. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h4)

question: What is the legal implication if you forget to chart a nursing care entry?

options.A: The hospital automatically wins any civil lawsuit
options.B: The doctor takes full responsibility for the missing note
options.C: The care is legally presumed not to have been performed
options.D: The nurse receives a bonus for saving paper

explanation: That's right! In a court of law, if it isn't documented, it legally didn't happen. Always chart promptly! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h5)

question: You realize you forgot to document a vital medication given two hours ago. What should you do?

options.A: Leave it out entirely because late charting is illegal
options.B: Write a late entry clearly labeled with the current time and the actual time of the event
options.C: Wait until the end of the month and add it to the file
options.D: Squeeze the note between previous lines and backdate your signature

explanation: Spot on! Always write a clear 'late entry' with the correct times. Never backdate or try to squeeze notes between lines. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four required elements to prove malpractice?

options.A: Actual physical or financial damages suffered
options.B: Breach of the established standard of care
options.C: Guaranteed financial recovery for the patient's family
options.D: Direct connection between the breach and the injury

explanation: Correct! Financial payout is a possible result of a successful lawsuit, not a baseline legal requirement to prove malpractice occurred. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h6)

question: What is the main difference between nursing malpractice and ordinary negligence?

options.A: Malpractice only happens when a patient dies in the ICU
options.B: Ordinary negligence can only be committed by doctors
options.C: Malpractice involves specialized professional skills and breaches of professional standards
options.D: Ordinary negligence carries heavier criminal prison sentences in Nigeria

explanation: You got it! Malpractice specifically applies when a licensed professional's specialized care falls below their training standards. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h6)

question: What is the primary role of a nurse acting as a patient advocate?

options.A: Refusing to talk with doctors about care plans
options.B: Suing the hospital administration whenever there is a treatment delay
options.C: Protecting the patient's rights, safety, and dignity when they cannot speak for themselves
options.D: Making all final medical decisions on behalf of the family

explanation: Brilliant! Being an advocate means standing up for your patients and keeping their best interests at heart. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h7)

question: You notice a family member pressuring a heavily sedated patient to sign a document. What is your best first step as an advocate?

options.A: Discharge the patient immediately from the ward
options.B: Ignore it because family financial matters are none of your business
options.C: Intervene to stop the activity and notify the nurse-in-charge or security
options.D: Help the family member hold the pen to finish quickly

explanation: Spot on! Protecting vulnerable, incapacitated patients from exploitation is a core part of your duty as a nurse. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T12#GNS321_U2_T12_h7)

question: What is the main focus of critical care in the community setting?

options.A: Conducting clinical drug trials in large urban tertiary hospitals
options.B: Performing complex elective surgeries in rural primary health centers
options.C: Delivering life-saving interventions outside traditional hospital intensive care units
options.D: Managing chronic stable illnesses during routine home visits

explanation: You don't always need a big hospital ICU to save a life! Community critical care is all about bringing quick emergency help right to primary clinics and homes. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h1)

question: Why is the community nurse so vital in settings with limited resources?

options.A: They replace the need for any secondary or tertiary healthcare facilities
options.B: They have unlimited access to advanced mechanical ventilators and dialysis machines
options.C: They serve as the first line of defense to stabilize rapidly deteriorating patients before hospital transfer
options.D: They are the only healthcare workers legally permitted to perform major surgeries

explanation: Spotting danger signs early and starting care right away makes all the difference when a patient arrives at a local clinic first. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h1)

question: On the AVPU neurological scale, what does the letter 'V' stand for?

options.A: Voice
options.B: Ventilation
options.C: Vomiting
options.D: Vascular

explanation: Remember AVPU: Alert, Voice-responsive, Pain-responsive, and Unresponsive. It's a quick and handy way to check mental status! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T13#GNS321_U2_T13_h2)
